  • Asked as: "Which has GAS / EBV as etiology?"; "autoimmune, young women, sun flares" → SLE.
  • Trap: the three "erythema M-" words. Still's vs SLE: both autoimmune; salmon + fever spikes = Still's.

A 12-year-old with recent sore throat now has migratory polyarthritis, a new murmur and chorea. Over his trunk are annular, polycyclic pink plaques that shift and disappear within a few hours. What is the etiology of this rash?

  1. Borrelia burgdorferi
  2. Group A Streptococcus
  3. Herpes simplex virus
  4. Mycoplasma pneumoniae

B. Erythema marginatum of rheumatic fever = GAS. Borrelia gives erythema migrans (single large ring lasting weeks); HSV/Mycoplasma give erythema multiforme targets.

B · Peripheral eruptions (palms & soles) HIGH-YIELD 2028 #77, #88, #89, #92 2027 #86–88, #95

Start acral, spread centripetally. Sexual contact + copper scaly palms = secondary syphilis; football-shaped erosions + oral erosions = HFMD; targets ≤2 cm = erythema multiforme.

A 24/M has fever and a rash on the trunk, palms and soles two months after unprotected sex. Which additional finding would argue AGAINST secondary syphilis?

  1. Copper-colored papules topped with scale
  2. Patchy "moth-eaten" hair loss
  3. Condyloma latum and mucous patches
  4. Tender vesicles on the palms evolving into erosions

D. Secondary syphilis is never vesicular in adults; tender palmar vesicles → erosions fit HFMD. A–C are all syphilis features.

C · Confluent desquamative erythemas (scarlatiniform look-alikes) MUST KNOW 2027 #90

Diffuse erythema then peeling. Sandpaper + Pastia's lines + strawberry tongue = scarlet fever; fissured lips + coronary vasculitis = Kawasaki; tender skin + Nikolsky, NO tongue signs = SSSS.

  • Asked as: long description (phage group II, Nikolsky, <10 y or renal dysfunction) → name it.

A 22/F has fever of 40°C, hypotension, conjunctival and oral mucosal erythema, and diffuse erythema that involves her palms. No deep soft-tissue infection is found; cultures show only colonization with a toxin-producing organism. Which toxin is most likely responsible?

  1. TSST-1
  2. Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin A from necrotizing fasciitis
  3. Exfoliative toxin of phage group II S. aureus
  4. Shiga toxin

A. Staph TSS: TSST-1, colonization only, fever >39°C, palms, mucosal erythema. Strep TSS needs severe GAS infection; phage group II = SSSS.

Both SSSS and TEN are Nikolsky (+). SSSS = toxin, child, superficial split, no mucosa. SJS/TEN = drug (80%), mucosa, whole-epidermis necrosis; graded by BSA: SJS <10% · overlap 10–30% · TEN >30%.

  • Asked as: "% necrosis" → SJS/overlap/TEN; "which favors TEN over SSSS".
  • Trap: Nikolsky is positive in BOTH; look at age, drug history, mucosa.

Both a 3-year-old and a 45-year-old have fever, painful skin and a positive Nikolsky sign. Which finding most favors TEN over SSSS in the adult?

  1. Diffuse erythema preceding the bullae
  2. Profound skin tenderness
  3. Oral and conjunctival erosions after starting allopurinol 3 weeks earlier
  4. Nasal and conjunctival secretions with irritability

C. Mucosal involvement + a new drug (allopurinol) = SJS/TEN. Tenderness and erythema occur in both; secretions/irritability are SSSS prodrome features.

New drug + fever + rash: plain exanthem (itchy, no organ damage) → DRESS (same rash + facial edema, eosinophilia, LIVER) → SJS/TEN (sloughing, mucosa). Febrile + new drug + tiny sterile pustules = AGEP.

  • DRESS genetics: can't detoxify arene oxides (anticonvulsants) or slow N-acetylators (sulfonamides).

A 28/M was started on cotrimoxazole 12 days ago. He now has an intensely pruritic, bright-red, symmetric maculopapular rash on trunk and limbs. He is alert and not prostrated; no facial edema, liver enzymes normal, no mucosal lesions or pustules. What is the most likely diagnosis?

  1. Drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
  2. Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis
  3. Measles
  4. Exanthematous drug-induced eruption

D. New drug + absence of prostration + very pruritic red rash, no organ involvement = simple exanthem. DRESS needs facial edema/hepatic involvement; AGEP needs pustules.

Mixed stages on the trunk = VARICELLA. Same stage, face + extremities incl. palms/soles = VARIOLA. Umbilicated "doughnut" pseudopustules on genitals/hands/face after intimate contact = MPOX. Painful GROUPED vesicles on red base = HSV.

During an outbreak investigation, a non-immune patient has fever, severe backache and vomiting, followed by deep pustules prominent on the face, forearms, palms and soles. In any one region, all lesions are at the same stage. Which agent is most likely?

  1. Varicella-zoster virus
  2. Rickettsia akari
  3. Variola major virus
  4. Pseudomonas aeruginosa

C. Same-stage lesions + face/extremities incl. palms/soles + backache = smallpox. Varicella has mixed stages and is trunk-predominant.

Mpox: test, infectivity, isolation HIGH-YIELD LECTURER 2028 #85 2027 #91, #92 quiz Q1

Test = PCR for viral DNA from the LESION (skin, fluid or crusts, vigorous swab). Infectious from symptom onset until the rash has FULLY healed with a FRESH layer of skin. Close contacts: 21 days.

  • Incubation 3–21 d (feels fine) → flu-like + lymphadenopathy 1–4 d before rash → rash → umbilicated pseudopustule → scale/ulcer → scab → heal. Illness lasts 2–4 wk.
  • Some people spread mpox 1–4 days before symptoms.
  • 4 routes: close/intimate contact (rash, scabs, saliva, respiratory secretions, sexual, prolonged face-to-face) · contaminated objects/fabrics · infected wild animals · pregnancy (fetus/newborn).
  • Patient: notify contacts, isolate for infectious period, don't share towels/glasses, disinfect shared spaces, cover upholstered furniture, mask + cover lesions.
  • Close contact: watch for symptoms; if none develop, complete 21 days isolation.
TRAP Scabbing/crusting = STILL contagious. Afebrile 24 h or symptom resolution is NOT the end point. Serology or blood tests are not the preferred test. (Trans also says "until lesions heal and scabs fall off"; the quiz/exam answer = fresh layer of skin.)
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: end of isolation; preferred specimen; cause of umbilicated genital pseudopustules after sex.
  • New angles to expect: contact quarantine length, incubation range, how to collect the specimen.

A clinician suspecting mpox in a man with umbilicated pustules on his genitals and thighs sends a serum antibody test and a throat swab. What is the BEST way to confirm the diagnosis?

  1. Repeat paired serum antibody titers in 2 weeks
  2. PCR for viral DNA on material vigorously swabbed from a skin lesion (fluid or crust)
  3. Tzanck smear of a vesicle base
  4. Blood PCR for viral load

B. Per trans, PCR of lesion material (skin, fluid, crusts) by vigorous swabbing is the test of choice. Antibodies only show exposure; blood is not the best specimen.

Raw oysters or seawater wound + cirrhosis + hemorrhagic bullae + hypotension = Vibrio vulnificus. Neutropenia + bulla → eschar with red halo in axilla/groin = ecthyma gangrenosum (Pseudomonas).

A. Neutropenia + axillary bulla → eschar with red halo = ecthyma gangrenosum (Pseudomonas). Vibrio needs seafood/seawater + cirrhosis.

A 48/F with acute myeloid leukemia receiving G-CSF develops fever and multiple tender, red-blue, very edematous plaques on her face, neck and arms that look almost blistered. CBC shows leukocytosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?

  1. Erythema nodosum
  2. Urticarial vasculitis
  3. Sweet syndrome
  4. Bacillary angiomatosis

C. Edematous pseudovesicular plaques on face/neck/arms + leukocytosis + hematologic cancer/G-CSF = Sweet. EN is on the shins in younger women.

G · Purpuric: meningococcemia vs RMSF vs dengue vs DGI HIGH-YIELD LECTURER

Fever + petechiae that multiply fast + hypotension = treat as bacterial sepsis NOW (acute meningococcemia; can't reliably tell from RMSF or echovirus 9). Purpura fulminans = DIC = emergency.

Acute meningococcemiaRMSFDengue
Agent / vectorN. meningitidisR. rickettsii (tick)Dengue virus (Aedes)
HostChildren, asplenia, C5–C8 deficiencyTick exposureTropics
Rash coursePink blanching MP/urticaria → numerous petechiae (trunk, limbs) → ± purpura fulminansWrists/ankles → centripetal; palms/soles late; macules → petechiaeFlushing → MP → petechiae after defervescence
SyndromeHypotension, meningitisHeadache, myalgia, abdominal pain; mortality up to 40%Breakbone pain, leukopenia, saddleback
DiseaseEtiologyMorphologyClueLook-alike
Purpura fulminansSevere DIC (sepsis, malignancy, trauma)Large irregular ecchymoses → hemorrhagic bullae → black necrosisEmergency; asplenia high riskRetiform purpura
Chronic meningococcemiaN. meningitidisMixed; purpura with pale blue-gray centers; leg nodules NOT tenderComplement deficiency, intermittent fever, arthritisEN, DGI
DGIN. gonorrhoeaeSparse, countable (<40) hemorrhagic pustules with gray necrotic centers near joints (upper ext.)Sexually active women; tenosynovitisChronic meningococcemia
Enteroviral petechialEchovirus 9, coxsackie A9Disseminated petechiaeOutbreaks; aseptic meningitisMeningococcemia
Viral hemorrhagic feverArena-, bunya-, filo- (Ebola), flavivirusesPetechiaeTravel; fever + shock + mucosal/GI bleedingDengue
TTP/HUSADAMTS13, Shiga toxin (E. coli O157:H7), drugsPetechiaeMAHA, low platelets, renal, neuro; normal coagulationDIC
Small-vessel vasculitis / HSPGAS, hep B/C, drugs; IgA (HSP)Palpable purpura in crops, dependent legsHSP: child + purpura + arthritis + abdominal pain—
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: host (asplenia, complement deficiency, sexually active) + purpuric pattern → organism; "next step" → treat as sepsis.
  • Trap: TTP/HUS coagulation is NORMAL; purpura fulminans = DIC.

A 23/F, sexually active, has low-grade fever, pain along the extensor tendons of her wrist, and about a dozen scattered hemorrhagic pustules with gray necrotic centers near her wrists and fingers. What is the most likely etiology?

  1. Neisseria meningitidis
  2. Neisseria gonorrhoeae
  3. Rickettsia rickettsii
  4. Echovirus 9

B. Sparse (<40) hemorrhagic pustules with gray centers near joints + tenosynovitis = DGI. Chronic meningococcemia can look alike but lacks tenosynovitis/sexual clue.

H · Ulcers & eschars: tularemia vs anthrax (and every eschar) MUST KNOW quiz Q5

Tender necrotic ulcer with raised borders (ulceroglandular) = TULAREMIA. Painless ulcer ringed by vesicles → black eschar with edema, NO other rash = ANTHRAX.

DiseaseEtiologyLesionExposureOther rash?
TularemiaFrancisella tularensisTender papule → tender necrotic ulcer, raised bordersTicks, biting flies, infected animals35% have other eruptions
AnthraxBacillus anthracisPruritic papule → 1 × 3 cm painless ulcer + vesicles → central eschar with edema → scarAnimals/animal products, sporesNone — eschar is the only lesion
Scrub typhusO. tsutsugamushiEscharMitesTruncal macular
Spotted feversR. africae etc.EscharTicksMP proximal limbs → trunk
RickettsialpoxR. akariEscharMouse mitesPapulovesicles
SodokuS. minusEscharRat biteBlotchy violaceous
Ecthyma gangrenosumP. aeruginosaEschar with red haloNeutropenia—
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: lesion + animal exposure → organism.
  • Trap: tender = tularemia; painless = anthrax; eschar + generalized rash = rickettsial.

A 40/M who processes goat hides noticed an itchy papule on his forearm that became a painless ulcer ringed by small vesicles, then a black central eschar with marked surrounding edema. He has no other skin lesions. Which organism is responsible?

  1. Francisella tularensis
  2. Rickettsia akari
  3. Orientia tsutsugamushi
  4. Bacillus anthracis

D. Painless ulcer + vesicle ring + eschar with edema as the ONLY skin finding + animal hides = anthrax. Tularemia's ulcer is tender; rickettsial eschars come with a rash.

Clue word → diagnosis (one-liners) HIGH-YIELD

Her stems are built from these phrases. See the phrase, say the disease.

Clue wordDiagnosisClue wordDiagnosis

EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "Which pair is INCORRECT?" across these phrases.
  • Trap: strawberry tongue appears in BOTH scarlet fever and Kawasaki; Pastia's lines only in scarlet fever.

Which clue–diagnosis pair is INCORRECT?

  1. "Grains of sand" on buccal mucosa opposite the premolars – measles
  2. Football-shaped erosions on palms and soles – hand-foot-and-mouth disease
  3. Accentuated petechiae in linear skin folds (Pastia's lines) – Kawasaki disease
  4. "Dewdrops on a rose petal" in mixed stages – varicella

C. Pastia's lines are scarlet fever. Kawasaki's signature is fissured lips, hand/foot edema and coronary vasculitis.

Practice drill — Dr. Co-Buenviaje style

A 29/M has 5 days of fever, myalgia and tender inguinal and cervical nodes, followed by the lesions shown, also on his genitals. Lesions are firm, some with central depression. His partner of the last month has similar lesions. His asymptomatic housemate asks how long he must stay isolated if he never develops symptoms. What is the correct advice?

  1. Until 24 hours without fever
  2. Complete 21 days of isolation
  3. Until the patient's lesions have crusted
  4. No isolation is needed without symptoms

B. Mpox close contact: isolate while watching for symptoms; if none develop, complete 21 days (= maximum incubation). Crusting is still contagious for the patient.

A 6-year-old has 2 days of low fever and dry cough, then the intensely itchy eruption shown, which began on the face and is now densest on the trunk. Which feature best distinguishes this from smallpox?

  1. Lesions in different stages (macules, vesicles, crusts) are present together
  2. Lesions are most prominent on the palms and soles
  3. Lesions are all at the same stage in one area
  4. Red macules on the tongue and palate appear first

A. Varicella = all stages at once, trunk-predominant. B, C and D describe variola.

A 17/M had a painful cluster of vesicles on his lip one week ago. He now has the symmetric lesions shown (≤2 cm, central dusky zone, pale ring, outer red rim) on his elbows, knees, palms and soles, with no skin sloughing. Which is the most likely trigger?

  1. Borrelia burgdorferi
  2. Group A Streptococcus
  3. Treponema pallidum
  4. Herpes simplex virus

D. Target lesions = erythema multiforme; recent herpes labialis = HSV trigger. Borrelia → erythema migrans (single ~15 cm ring); GAS → erythema marginatum.

A 61/M with alcoholic cirrhosis develops fever, hypotension and the lesions shown, a day after a seaside trip where he ate raw oysters. The lesions are evolving into necrotic ulcers. Which organism is most likely?

  1. Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  2. Staphylococcus aureus
  3. Vibrio vulnificus
  4. Neisseria meningitidis

C. Raw oysters + cirrhosis + hemorrhagic bullae → necrotic ulcers + shock = disseminated V. vulnificus (50% mortality). Pseudomonas ecthyma is a neutropenia lesion.

A 4-year-old and his sister had mild fever, sore mouth and the lesions shown. Six weeks later the mother returns worried about a new finding. Which late finding is expected from this illness?

  1. Shedding of the fingernails (onychomadesis)
  2. Splinter hemorrhages under the nails
  3. "Moth-eaten" alopecia
  4. Coronary artery aneurysm

A. HFMD (coxsackie A16/EV71): onychomadesis 1–2 months later. Moth-eaten alopecia = secondary syphilis; coronary aneurysm = Kawasaki.

A 52/M started allopurinol 3 weeks ago. He has fever, purpuric targetoid macules, oral erosions and a positive Nikolsky sign. Using his palm, detached skin (bullae, erosions) equals 6 palms and Nikolsky-positive skin not yet blistered equals 8 palms. What is the classification?

  1. Stevens-Johnson syndrome
  2. SJS/TEN overlap
  3. Toxic epidermal necrolysis
  4. Erythema multiforme major

B. Detached + detachable = 6 + 8 = 14% (palm = 1%) → 10–30% = overlap. Counting only detached (6%) would wrongly give SJS.

Which eruption–drug pair is INCORRECT?

  1. Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis – antimicrobials
  2. DRESS – aromatic anticonvulsants
  3. SJS/TEN – allopurinol
  4. Erythema migrans – penicillin

D. Erythema migrans is Lyme (B. burgdorferi); penicillin is listed for erythema MULTIFORME. Don't mix the "erythema M-" names.

A 26-week pregnant woman's husband just returned from a tropical area with Zika transmission. He has a pruritic maculopapular rash, conjunctival injection and small-joint arthralgia. Apart from Aedes mosquito bites, which route puts the fetus at risk through him?

  1. Shared saliva
  2. Fecal-oral contact
  3. Sexual transmission
  4. Water contaminated with animal urine

C. Zika: Aedes; less commonly sexual or transfusion; maternal spread → microcephaly. Shared saliva = roseola; urine-contaminated water = leptospirosis.

A 38/F back from a safari in southern Africa has fever, headache, regional lymphadenopathy, a black crusted lesion with a red rim on her ankle where a tick was attached, and a maculopapular rash on her proximal limbs spreading to her trunk. Which is the most likely etiology?

  1. Orientia tsutsugamushi
  2. Rickettsia africae
  3. Rickettsia akari
  4. Bacillus anthracis

B. Tick + Africa + eschar + MP rash proximal limbs → trunk = African tick-bite fever (spotted fever). Orientia = mites in Asia; R. akari = urban mouse mites; anthrax has no rash.

A 9-year-old with asplenia has 12 hours of fever and lethargy, BP 80/40, and a petechial eruption on the trunk and legs that is increasing by the hour. There is no travel or tick history. What is the best next step?

  1. Wait for blood culture results before antibiotics
  2. Skin biopsy to separate meningococcemia from RMSF
  3. Treat immediately as bacterial sepsis
  4. Observe whether the rash reaches the palms and soles

C. Lecturer point: meningococcemia, RMSF and echovirus 9 may be impossible to tell apart quickly. Treat as bacterial sepsis; asplenia raises the risk of purpura fulminans.

A febrile woman with Sjögren's syndrome has hive-like plaques. All of the following support urticarial vasculitis EXCEPT:

  1. Each lesion resolves completely within 24 hours
  2. Lesions do not blanch under a glass slide
  3. Lesions burn rather than only itch
  4. Individual lesions persist for 3–5 days

A. ≤24 h lesions = classic urticaria. Urticarial vasculitis lasts 3–5 d, doesn't blanch (extravasated blood) and may burn.

Which pairing of rash timing and disease is INCORRECT?

  1. Roseola – rash appears after the fever resolves
  2. Still's disease – rash coincides with fever spikes
  3. Dengue – petechiae after defervescence
  4. Relapsing fever – rash at the onset of each febrile episode

D. Relapsing fever (Borrelia) has a central rash at the END of the febrile episode.

A 45/F from the southern US recalls removing a Lone Star tick (Amblyomma americanum) a week ago. She has mild malaise and one annular lesion with central clearing about 8 cm across. Compared with the leading alternative, what is her diagnosis?

  1. Southern tick-associated rash illness (STARI)
  2. Lyme disease
  3. Erythema marginatum
  4. Erythema multiforme

A. Lone Star tick, smaller (~8 cm) lesion, bite recalled, milder illness = STARI. Lyme EM averages 15 cm, Ixodes.

A kindergarten teacher who is 16 weeks pregnant was exposed to a 6-year-old with the rash shown, which appeared after the child's fever subsided. What fetal complication is she most at risk for?

  1. Microcephaly, congenital heart disease, deafness
  2. Coronary artery aneurysm
  3. Neonatal flaccid paralysis
  4. Fetal hydrops

D. Slapped cheeks + lacy rash = parvovirus B19 → fetal hydrops. A = congenital rubella (and Zika microcephaly).

A 4-year-old with nasal colonization by toxin-producing S. aureus has fever, irritability and diffusely red, extremely tender skin. Light lateral pressure forms bullae. He has no strawberry tongue and no circumoral pallor. Compared with TEN, where is the split in his skin and what causes it?

  1. Entire epidermis; drug hypersensitivity
  2. Superficial epidermis; toxin from S. aureus phage group II
  3. Dermal–epidermal junction; group A strep exotoxins
  4. Superficial epidermis; viral cytopathic effect

B. SSSS: toxin-mediated, superficial cleavage; TEN is deeper/whole epidermis and drug-induced. Missing tongue signs exclude scarlet fever.

Last-look cram sheet

  • 8 types: central MP (most common) · peripheral · confluent desquamative · vesiculobullous · urticaria-like · nodular · purpuric · ulcer/eschar.
  • Measles: paramyxo, trunk 2–3 d, 3–5 d, Koplik. Rubella: toga, trunk 1 d, clears, 2–3 d, postauricular, congenital microcephaly/CHD/deafness.
  • Fifth: B19, slapped cheeks → lacy, hydrops, transfusion. Roseola: HHV-6/7, <3 y, after fever, face spared, shared saliva.
  • Transmission: varicella airborne · HFMD oral-oral/fecal-oral · typhoid food/water · lepto animal-urine water · Zika Aedes + sex.
  • Dengue: flushing → MP → petechiae after defervescence. Still's: salmon at fever spikes. Relapsing fever: end of episode.
  • Lice = epidemic typhus · flea = murine · mite = scrub (eschar) · mouse mite = rickettsialpox · Ixodes = Lyme 15 cm · Lone Star = STARI 8 cm.
  • RMSF wrists/ankles → centripetal; syphilis copper scaly palms, never vesicular; HFMD football erosions + onychomadesis; EM targets ≤2 cm.
  • Osler tender (subacute viridans) · Janeway painless (acute S. aureus). COVID: chilblains (mild), retiform purpura (severe).
  • Scarlet: sandpaper, Pastia, circumoral pallor · Kawasaki: idiopathic, coronary · Staph TSS: TSST-1, colonization · SSSS: tender, Nikolsky, no tongue signs.
  • SJS <10 · overlap 10–30 · TEN >30%; palm = 1%; detached + detachable. Allopurinol, anticonvulsants, antibiotics.
  • DRESS: anticonvulsant/sulfa + facial edema + eosinophilia + liver. AGEP: new drug + fever + sterile pustules. EBV + ampicillin 30–90%.
  • Varicella mixed stages, trunk · smallpox same stage, palms/soles · mpox umbilicated + nodes · HSV painful grouped.
  • Mpox: PCR of lesion swab; infectious until fresh skin forms; contacts 21 d; incubation 3–21 d.
  • Raw oysters + cirrhosis = Vibrio · neutropenia + eschar red halo = ecthyma (Pseudomonas) · hot tub = Pseudomonas folliculitis.
  • Urticarial vasculitis: 3–5 d, non-blanching, burning, hep B/SLE. EN: tender shins, young women, OCPs. Sweet: edematous plaques, leukocytosis, G-CSF.
  • Meningococcemia: asplenia/C5–C8 → treat as sepsis. Purpura fulminans = DIC. DGI <40 gray-centered pustules + tenosynovitis. TTP/HUS normal coags.
  • Tularemia tender ulcer · anthrax painless eschar, no other rash.
  • Rat-bite fever ≠ Borrelia (past key error): Spirillum minus / Streptobacillus moniliformis.

2.04 PE of the Skin / General Approach to Skin Disorders 19 items

Dr. Gilbert C. Yang · Recall 3 / Comp 4 / App 8 / Analysis 4 · Past-exam style source: 2028 LE2 #57–75 AND 2027 LE2 #59–77 (same professor all years) · Main source: 2026 trans 2.04 (25 pp.)

How Dr. Yang asks
  • Short case → name the lesion. Primary or secondary, decided by size cutoff (1 cm; 0.5 cm for purpura; 5 cm for tumor). 2028 gave the same case twice, changing only 3 mm vs 3 cm (vesicle vs bulla).
  • Sign → disease or depth. Auspitz, Darier, Nikolsky, Asboe-Hansen, dimple. "Negative Nikolsky → subepidermal."
  • "Which pair is INCORRECT?" sign–disease or test–disease (asked in both 2027 and 2028).
  • Picture matching: lesion photos (crust, scale, nodule, scar, ulcer, telangiectasia, wheal, pustule) and nail photos (pitting, half-and-half).
  • Clue word → diagnosis: exclamation-point hairs, carpet tacks, CKD nails, steroid cream → atrophy, leprosy → anesthesia, farmer → linear.
Past-exam concept map (2027 / 2028)
Concept20282027Covered in
Primary lesion by size (vesicle vs bulla)#61, #62—Size cutoffs
Primary lesion definitions / pictures (wheal, pustule, nodule)#69–70#75–76Primary lesions
Primary lesion = main diagnostic tool—#62Approach
Secondary lesions (ulcer, lichenification, fissure, scales, crust)#57, #69–70#59, #60, #61Secondary lesions

Atrophy from topical steroid—#72Atrophy

Incorrect sign–disease pair#68#69, #71Bedside signs
KOH ("spaghetti/ziti and meatballs"), patch test#72#67Lab tests
Leprosy symptom (anesthesia)#65—Leprosy
Vitiligo association (thyroid)—#70Color disorders
Alopecia areata (exclamation-point hairs); cicatricial (DLE)#58, #59#65Hair / alopecia
Nails: psoriasis, CKD (half-and-half), pictures#60#68, #73–74Nails
Psoriasis secondary lesion (scales)#57#69Psoriasis capsule
Ichthyosis vulgaris; pityriasis rosea#66#64NOT in 2026 trans (see trap box in Arrangement)

Primary lesions: flat, raised, fluid HIGH-YIELD 2028 #61–62, #69 2027 #75–76

Primary lesion = the ORIGINAL lesion of the disease. Sort it by: flat or raised? solid or fluid? then SIZE (1 cm).

FamilyLesionSizeDefining featureLecture example
Flat (not palpable)Macule< 1 cmColor change onlyFreckles
Patch≥ 1 cmBig macule—
Raised, solidPapule< 1 cmCircumscribed solid elevationLichen planus
Plaque≥ 1 cmFlat-topped, plateau-likePsoriasis
Nodule≥ 1 cmDomed, deep ("deep papule"), solid or cysticBasal cell CA
Tumor> 5 cmLarge solid mass, mobile or fixedSquamous cell CA
EdematousWhealAnyPale-red edematous plateau, gone in 24–48 h (evanescent)Urticaria / allergy
Fluid-filledVesicle< 1 cmSerous, clear or hemorrhagic fluidChickenpox
Bulla≥ 1 cmSame fluid, bigger—
PustuleAnyVisible pus (white/yellow/green); may form "lakes"—
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "fluid-filled lesions measuring X" → name it; or a definition in Column A matched to a photo (2027 #75 wheal = "short-lived edema").
  • Trap: wheal vs plaque → how to tell: wheal is evanescent (lesions come and go within a day).
  • Trap: pustule vs vesicle → pus (white/yellow) = pustule regardless of size.

A 26/F develops itchy, pale-red, raised, swollen lesions of various sizes and shapes after eating shrimp. Each lesion fades within hours, and new ones appear elsewhere. What is the primary lesion?

  1. Plaque
  2. Wheal
  3. Patch
  4. Bulla

B. Edematous, pale-red, changes shape, gone within 24–48 h = wheal (urticaria). A plaque is a fixed solid plateau that persists.

Size cutoffs: the near-miss items HIGH-YIELD 2028 #61 vs #62

1 cm splits each pair. 5 cm makes a tumor. 0.5 cm splits petechiae from purpura. READ THE UNIT (mm vs cm).

PairSmallerCutoffBigger
FlatMacule1 cmPatch
Solid raisedPapule1 cmPlaque (flat top) or nodule (domed, deep)
Solid massNodule5 cmTumor (> 5 cm)
FluidVesicle1 cmBulla
Blood in skin (non-blanching)Petechiae0.5 cmPurpura
No cutoffWheal (any size), pustule (any size; defined by pus)
TRAP 2028 #61 and #62 were the same 22/M with fever and painful fluid-filled lesions at the mouth angles; only "3 mm" (vesicle) vs "3 cm" (bulla) changed. Circle the number AND the unit before reading the choices.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: a size in mm or cm plus "flat / raised / fluid / pus".
  • Trap: plaque vs nodule (both ≥ 1 cm) → how to tell: plaque is a flat plateau (psoriasis); nodule is domed and deep (BCC).

A 28/F has multiple light-brown lesions on the trunk. They cannot be felt on palpation. The smallest is 4 mm; the one being described measures 3 cm. What is the primary lesion being described?

  1. Macule
  2. Plaque
  3. Patch
  4. Nodule

C. Not palpable = flat; ≥ 1 cm = patch. The 4-mm ones would be macules (near-miss).

Secondary lesions HIGH-YIELD 2028 #57, #69–70 2027 #59–61

Secondary lesion = what a primary lesion BECOMES (natural course, scratching, infection). 9 types.

LesionWhat it isClue word → example
ScalesFlakes of stratum corneumSilvery scales → psoriasis (sheds in 5 days vs 28)
CrustDried serum, blood, pusHoney-colored → impetigo 📌 (yellow = serum, green = pus, brown/dark red = blood)
LichenificationThick skin, accentuated skin linesRepeated rubbing/scratching (chronic itch)
ExcoriationPunctate or linear abrasionFingernail scratching → atopic dermatitis
ErosionLoss of epidermis onlySuperficial burn/sunburn; no scar
UlcerInto dermis or deeperLeg ulcer; heals with scar
ScarFibrous tissue replacing a defectHypertrophic/hard or atrophic/soft; keloid = claw-like extension beyond the wound
FissureLinear crack, painfulPalms/soles (thick, least expandable corneum), dry lips
AtrophyThinning; loss of substance under intact epidermisPotent topical steroid (clobetasol)
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: a symptom story → name the secondary lesion (2027: hair dye + thick lined skin = lichenification; painful sole cracks = fissure).
  • Trap: lichenification vs scales → how to tell: lichenification = thick skin with deep lines; scales = loose flakes on the surface.
  • Trap: excoriation vs fissure → excoriation is a scratch (fingernail); fissure is a crack from tension/dryness.

A 6/M with atopic dermatitis scratches his antecubital folds at night. PE shows several superficial straight-line abrasions, some with pinpoint dried blood. What secondary lesion is this?

  1. Fissures
  2. Lichenification
  3. Erosions
  4. Excoriations

D. Linear abrasions made by fingernails = excoriations. Lichenification needs chronic rubbing with thickened, lined skin; fissures are cracks from tension.

Erosion vs ulcer vs scar HIGH-YIELD 2027 #59, #77 2028 #73–75

Did the defect reach the DERMIS? No → erosion, no scar. Yes → ulcer, heals with scar.

ErosionUlcerScarKeloid
DepthEpidermis onlyDermis ± subcutisFibrous tissue filling an old defectHypertrophic scar
HealsNo scarScar—Grows beyond the wound (claw-like)
ExampleSunburn, ruptured blisterLeg ulcer, pressure ulcerHealed woundKeloid
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "loss of epidermis AND dermis, heals with scarring" or picture matching (scar, ulcer, keloid, telangiectasia).
  • Trap: keloid vs ordinary hypertrophic scar → keloid extends into unaffected skin.

A 19/M's sunburn blisters ruptured, leaving shallow, moist, red, weeping areas on the shoulders. Which statement about these lesions is CORRECT?

  1. They are erosions and are expected to heal without scarring
  2. They are ulcers and will heal with a scar
  3. They are fissures caused by decreased skin elasticity
  4. They are primary lesions, since they appeared within days

A. Loss of epidermis only = erosion → no scar. An ulcer needs dermal loss. Erosions are secondary lesions (from ruptured vesicles/bullae).

Atrophy from topical steroids HIGH-YIELD 2027 #72

OTC "cream" secretly containing a potent steroid (clobetasol) for 1–2 weeks → ATROPHY, which is IRREVERSIBLE.

  • Atrophy = diminished skin layers: epidermis intact, substance lost underneath.
  • Epidermal atrophy: thin, shiny, "cigarette-paper wrinkling".
  • Dermal atrophy: loss of connective tissue → depressed lesion.
  • No treatment reverses it p. 4.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: self-medication with topical steroid / whitening or "anti-itch" cream → what lesion results.
  • Trap: purpura or crust as distractors; also "reversible after stopping" (wrong).

A 32/F applied a friend's "anti-itch cream" to a facial rash daily for 3 weeks. The skin is now thin, shiny and finely wrinkled like cigarette paper. The cream contained clobetasol. Which statement is TRUE?

  1. This is lichenification from repeated rubbing
  2. The change resolves fully within weeks after stopping the cream
  3. This is epidermal atrophy and it is irreversible
  4. This is an erosion and will heal without scarring

C. Potent steroid → atrophy; the trans says it is irreversible with no treatment. Lichenification is thickening, the opposite.

Special lesions + diascopy (blanch or not) HIGH-YIELD 2027 #63 2028 #74

Press a glass slide (diascopy): ERYTHEMA (dilated capillaries) blanches; PURPURA/PETECHIAE (blood outside vessels) do NOT.

LesionDefinitionClue
PetechiaePurpuric macules, usually grouped< 0.5 cm; non-blanching
PurpuraBleeding into skin (macule → plaque)≥ 0.5 cm; non-blanching. Palpable purpura → comprehensive ROS (systemic disease)
TelangiectasiaDilated superficial vesselsLegs; lecturer: also does not blanch
CystCavity whose lining makes its contentsRecurs → enucleate whole capsule (epidermal inclusion cyst)
ComedoneKeratin plug in follicle openingAcne vulgaris. Closed = whitehead; open = blackhead
  • Diascopy also shows glassy yellow-brown papules = apple-jelly sign → sarcoidosis (also skin TB, lymphoma, granuloma annulare).
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "which test tells if red lesions are from vessel inflammation/bleeding" → diascopy (2027 #63, HSP). New angles: which lesion blanches; petechiae vs purpura by size.
  • Trap: tourniquet test or patch test as distractors → diascopy is the glass-slide bedside test.

On diascopy, which of the following lesions is expected to BLANCH?

  1. Grouped 2-mm petechiae on the legs of a patient with low platelets
  2. Erythematous macules of a viral exanthem
  3. 1.5-cm purpuric patches on the shins
  4. Telangiectasia on the thighs

B. Erythema = capillary dilatation → blanches. Petechiae and purpura are extravasated blood; the lecturer said telangiectasia also does not blanch.

Approach and how to state the derm PE LECTURER 2027 #62

In derm, do the PE FIRST, then a focused history. The primary lesion is the main basis of the differential diagnosis.

  • Flow: chief complaint → PE 📌 → detailed history (focused on the PE findings) → impression → tests → plan p. 2.
  • Light: natural sunlight is ideal. Inspect the whole skin incl. scalp, hair, nails, mucosa, palms, soles, web spaces. Chaperone when undressing.
  • Always check palms and soles: copper-colored lesions ("dimes, nickels") → ask sexual history (secondary syphilis). Check lymph nodes in suspected infection or malignancy.
  • Sentence order: Number → Arrangement → Margination → Color → Shape → Primary → Secondary → Location/distribution. Solitary → skip arrangement. Do not start with the primary lesion.
Trans sample caseStatement (key words)
ChickenpoxMultiple erythematous round macules, papules and vesicles with surrounding erythema, disseminated on back and nape
Impetigo…erythematous plaques with erosions topped with scales and yellowish-brown crusts, grouped on the chin
PsoriasisWell-defined erythematous oval plaques, thick silvery-white scales, bilateral elbows
Tinea corporisSolitary … round annular plaque with prominent border and central clearing, scales, on the arm
Pityriasis versicolorMultiple coalescing well-defined hypopigmented oval thin plaques with fine scales
Herpes zoster (Table 14)Multiple, grouped … vesicles on erythematous base, dermatomal (T10), unilateral
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "main diagnostic tool" (primary lesion); "which comes first" (PE); "which statement follows the correct order".
  • Trap: "detailed history first" (true elsewhere in medicine, not derm).

Which description of a 40/M's rash follows the recommended order for stating a dermatologic PE?

  1. Plaques, multiple, erythematous, well-defined, with scales, on the knees
  2. On the knees, multiple well-defined plaques, erythematous, topped with scales
  3. Erythematous scales on multiple plaques, well-defined, on the knees
  4. Multiple, well-defined, erythematous, oval plaques topped with scales on the knees

D. Number → margination → color → shape → primary → secondary → location. A starts with the primary lesion (what the lecturer said not to do).

Shape, arrangement, distribution: clue words MUST KNOW 2027 #66

The pattern points to the disease: clustered = herpes; linear = plants/thorns; dermatomal = zoster; palms and soles = secondary syphilis.

ClueTermThink
Clustered togetherHerpetiform (grouped)Herpes simplex / zoster
In a line, gardener/farmerLinearPlant contact / thorn trauma
BullseyeIris / targetoidErythema multiforme
Ring, central clearingAnnularTinea corporis (sample case)
Central dimple ("pimple na may dimple")UmbilicatedMolluscum contagiosum
Snake-likeSerpiginousElastosis perforans serpiginosa
Scattered discreteDisseminatedChickenpox
Merge togetherConfluentMeasles (viral exanthem); non-confluent = molluscum
One spinal nerve areaDermatomalHerpes zoster
Flexures / extensorsFlexor / extensorAtopic dermatitis / psoriasis
Trunk + palms and soles, copper-colored—Secondary syphilis → sexual history
Scalp—Seborrheic dermatitis (extensive/refractory → think HIV)
  • Extent: patient's palm ≈ 1% BSA. Psoriasis mild < 3%, moderate 3–10%, severe > 10%.
NOT IN 2026 TRANS 2027 #64 asked pityriasis rosea ("drooping pine-tree" / Christmas-tree pattern on trunk cleavage lines) and 2028 #66 asked ichthyosis vulgaris (fine plate-like scales on shins in an atopic patient, keyed from Fitzpatrick). Neither is in the current trans; know the one-liners only.

A 24/M has a rash on the trunk and copper-colored scaly papules on both palms and soles. After completing the skin exam, which part of the history is MOST important to take next?

  1. Sexual history
  2. Occupational exposure to plants
  3. Family history of atopy
  4. Recent use of topical steroids

A. Lecturer's boxed point: copper-colored palm/sole lesions → secondary syphilis → ask sexual history.

Nikolsky vs Asboe-Hansen; PV vs TEN HIGH-YIELD 2028 #63, #68 2027 #71

Both signs are POSITIVE when the split is ABOVE the basement membrane (pemphigus vulgaris, TEN). NEGATIVE Nikolsky with blisters → the split is SUBEPIDERMAL.

NikolskyAsboe-Hansen
Where you pressIntact / unblistered skinOn an existing bulla
DirectionLateral (sideways rub)Downward
Positive =Epidermis shears offBlister spreads sideways
Seen inPemphigus vulgaris, TEN (pathology above the BMZ)
Pemphigus vulgarisTEN
CauseAutoimmuneMainly drugs (cell-mediated, granulysin)
LevelSuprabasal acantholysis (intraepidermal)Widespread keratinocyte apoptosis → detachment
MucosaErosions almost always (oral, nasal)Involved
SkinFlaccid blisters, large erosions, spares palms/solesPurpuric macules → flaccid bullae → sheets detach; starts upper trunk
Signs(+) Nikolsky, (+) Asboe-Hansen(+) Nikolsky
Numbers—Onset 4–28 days after drug; risk in first 8 wk. SJS < 10% · overlap 10–30% · TEN > 30% BSA
  • TEN drugs: cotrimoxazole, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, lamotrigine, nevirapine, allopurinol, meloxicam (oxicam).
  • Tense bullae in an elderly patient with (−) Nikolsky = subepidermal blister (e.g. bullous pemphigoid Harrison's; not named in trans).
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: sign → depth; maneuver described → name the sign; drug started X days ago + BSA % → SJS/overlap/TEN.
  • Trap: Nikolsky vs Asboe-Hansen → intact skin vs existing blister. 2027 #71 paired Asboe-Hansen with psoriasis (incorrect).
  • SSSS vs TEN is taught in 2.05 Fever and Rash, not in this trans.

A 38/M started carbamazepine 2 weeks ago. He now has painful dusky macules, flaccid bullae and sheets of detached epidermis over about 40% of his BSA, with oral erosions. Lateral pressure on normal-looking skin peels the epidermis. What is the diagnosis?

  1. Stevens-Johnson syndrome
  2. SJS-TEN overlap
  3. Toxic epidermal necrolysis
  4. Pemphigus vulgaris

C. Aromatic antiepileptic, onset 4–28 days, > 30% BSA = TEN. Overlap is 10–30%. PV is autoimmune, not drug-timed.

Bedside signs → disease ("incorrect pair" items) HIGH-YIELD 2028 #68 2027 #69, #71

Match the MANEUVER to the disease: scrape = psoriasis, rub = mastocytosis, pinch = dermatofibroma, press intact skin or bulla = PV/TEN.

SignManeuverPositiveDisease
AuspitzScrape off scale (blunt glass slide)Pinpoint bleedingPsoriasis (not specific)
DarierFirmly rub lesion (finger, pen end)Wheal confined to lesion, after minutesCutaneous mastocytosis / urticaria pigmentosa
Dimple (Fitzpatrick)Squeeze sideways (thumb + index)Lesion dimples inwardDermatofibroma
NikolskyLateral pressure, intact skinEpidermis shearsPV, TEN
Asboe-HansenDownward pressure on bullaBulla spreadsPV, TEN
KoebnerTrauma to normal skinNew lesions at injury sitePsoriasis, vitiligo, warts, molluscum
Apple-jellyDiascopyGlassy yellow-brownSarcoidosis
MUST KNOW 📌 Mastocytosis: AVOID mast-cell degranulators: alcohol, dextran, polymyxin-B, morphine, codeine, scopolamine, d-tubocurarine, aspirin, NSAIDs (young children can go into shock). p. 11
  • Dermatofibroma: firm, button-like dermal nodule 3–10 mm on extremities; late reaction to an arthropod bite.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "Which is the INCORRECT sign and disease?" (2028: Darier–TEN; 2027: Asboe-Hansen–psoriasis).
  • Trap: Darier sign (mastocytosis) is often wrongly paired with TEN or urticaria; Auspitz with PV.

A 35/F has a firm, 6-mm brown button-like nodule on the shin that appeared months after an insect bite. When the examiner squeezes the skin on either side of it, the lesion puckers downward. Which sign is this?

  1. Darier sign
  2. Auspitz sign
  3. Dimple (Fitzpatrick) sign
  4. Koebner phenomenon

C. Lateral compression → dimple from epidermis tethered to the dermal lesion = dermatofibroma. Darier needs rubbing and gives a wheal.

Psoriasis capsule (appears in every topic) HIGH-YIELD 2028 #57, #60 2027 #69, #73

Psoriasis = sharply marginated dull-red PLAQUES with silvery-white SCALES on EXTENSORS (elbows, knees, scalp), sparing the face; Auspitz +, Koebner +.

  • Mechanism: shortened keratinocyte cycle → 28x epidermal production → sheds in ~5 days (normal 28) → scales pile up.
  • Primary lesion = papules/plaques; secondary = scales.
  • Triggers: trauma, infection, medication. Psoriatic arthritis 10–25% → ask about joint pain (focused ROS).
  • Severity by BSA: mild < 3%, moderate 3–10%, severe > 10%. Severe forms: pustular, erythrodermic (fever).
  • Nails (25%): pitting = most frequent; oil spots = pathognomonic; onycholysis; subungual hyperkeratosis.

A 50/M with plaque psoriasis and joint pains has nail changes. Which nail finding is considered PATHOGNOMONIC of nail psoriasis?

  1. Salmon-colored "oil spots" under the nail plate
  2. Small, shallow pits on the nail plate
  3. Detachment of the nail plate from the distal nail bed
  4. Transverse grooves parallel to the lunula

A. Oil spots are pathognomonic; pitting is the MOST FREQUENT sign (near-miss). Transverse grooves = Beau lines.

Wood's lamp and other examination aids HIGH-YIELD LECTURER

Wood's lamp = long-wave UV (365 nm). Coral red = erythrasma; yellow-green = pityriasis versicolor; green-yellow = Microsporum. T. tonsurans does NOT glow. 📌

ConditionOrganismWood's lamp
Tinea capitis, ectothrixMicrosporum canis, M. audouiniiGreen to yellow
Tinea capitis, endothrix 📌Trichophyton tonsuransNo fluorescence (negative does not exclude tinea)
ErythrasmaCorynebacterium minutissimumCoral red
Pityriasis versicolorMalasseziaYellow-green
Vitiligo, melasma, CALMsMelanin changeContrast accentuated
AidUse
Hand lensFine detail: follicular plugging (lupus), Wickham striae (lichen planus), translucence/telangiectasia (BCC), gray-blue (melanoma)
Oblique light (dark room)Slight elevation or depression
Subdued lightHypo-/hyperpigmented contrast
Dermoscopy (10–30x)Benign vs malignant pigmented lesions
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: incorrect test–diagnosis pair; color → organism; "Wood's lamp negative, so is tinea excluded?"
  • Trap: coral red (erythrasma) vs yellow-green (PV): mnemonic Coral = Corynebacterium.

A 7/M has scaly patches with broken hairs on the scalp. His older brother was treated for Trichophyton tonsurans tinea capitis. Wood's lamp shows no fluorescence. What is the correct interpretation?

  1. Tinea capitis is excluded; consider seborrheic dermatitis
  2. The lamp is faulty, since all dermatophytes fluoresce green
  3. The finding suggests erythrasma
  4. Tinea capitis is not excluded, because T. tonsurans is an endothrix organism that does not fluoresce

D. Lecturer-pinned point: endothrix T. tonsurans does not glow; only ectothrix Microsporum does.

Lab tests: test → finding → disease HIGH-YIELD 2028 #72 2027 #67

KOH = fungi; Tzanck = herpesviruses; patch test = allergic contact dermatitis (gold standard); biopsy = tumors and blistering disease.

TestSample / howPositive findingDisease
KOH smear (10–20%)Scrape scales outward from advancing marginLong, narrow, septate, branching hyphaeDermatophytes (tinea)
Pseudohyphae + budding yeastCandida
"Ziti/spaghetti and meatballs": short hyphae + yeastPityriasis versicolor, Malassezia folliculitis
Tzanck smearBase of a fresh vesicle; Giemsa/WrightMultinucleated giant cells (10–12 nuclei)HSV, varicella, zoster
Patch test~35 allergens + 1 control, taped 48 h; final read 72 or 96 h+ to ++++Allergic contact dermatitis (type IV)
Gram stainCV → iodine → alcohol → safranin(+) purple, (−) redBacterial infection
CultureWedge biopsy, ½ histopath ½ culture; fungi on SabouraudOrganismBacteria, mycobacteria, fungi
Skin biopsy3–4 mm punch; formalin → H&E; Michel's medium → IFHistology / IFNeoplasm, bullous disease, unclear dx
  • KOH false negative ~15% → still treat if clinically suspected; culture before systemic therapy (onychomycosis).
  • Patch test allergens: nickel/cobalt, formaldehyde, fragrance, neomycin/bacitracin, latex, PPD (hair dye).
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: condition → test; smear description → diagnosis; "incorrect test–disease pair".
  • Trap: Tzanck vs KOH for vesicles → Tzanck is for herpes vesicles; KOH for scaly fungal lesions.

A 33/F hairdresser has itchy, scaly, lichenified dermatitis on both hands that flares after applying hair dye. You want to identify the specific allergen. Which test, and when is the FINAL reading done?

  1. KOH smear; read immediately
  2. Patch test; final read at the 72nd or 96th hour
  3. Tzanck smear; read after Giemsa staining
  4. Patch test; final read once the patches are removed at 48 hours

B. Patch testing is the gold standard for ACD (PPD in hair dye). Patches come off at 48 h, but the final delayed reading is at 72 or 96 h (D is the near-miss).

Leprosy: sensitivity testing + spectrum HIGH-YIELD 2028 #65

Every suspected leprosy lesion gets a SENSITIVITY evaluation: the nerves are already damaged when skin signs appear → hypesthetic/anesthetic, anhidrotic lesions.

FunctionHow tested
VasomotorAxon-reflex erythema (capillary dilatation)
SweatingIodine-starch test (expect ↓ sweating, not hyperhidrosis)
ThermalHot vs cold (~45 °C)
PainTip vs base of a needle
TouchCotton wisp or Semmes-Weinstein monofilament
Tuberculoid (TT)Lepromatous (LL)
Cell-mediated immunityGoodAbsent
LesionsFew, well-defined hypopigmented/erythematous hypesthetic plaques, raised edges, annularMany nodules, diffuse infiltration
ExtrasOne body segmentMadarosis, leonine facies, extensive nerve damage
  • M. leprae: obligate intracellular AFB, cannot be cultured in vitro (armadillo footpad). Spread by respiratory droplets. Incubation 2–40 y (usually 5–7).
  • Spectrum TT → BT → BB → BL → LL depends on CMI. Indeterminate: few hypopigmented macules. Disability persists after MDT.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: what symptom/finding accompanies the lesions (anesthesia); which test; TT vs LL by immunity.
  • Trap: hyperhidrosis or pruritus as distractors → leprosy gives LOSS of sweating and sensation.

A 45/M has multiple skin-colored nodules on the face and ears, thickened facial skin and loss of the lateral eyebrows. Which statement about his condition is CORRECT?

  1. He has a complete lack of cell-mediated immunity against the organism
  2. He has strong cell-mediated immunity, so lesions are few and well-defined
  3. The organism is readily cultured on Sabouraud agar
  4. Sensitivity testing is unnecessary because nerves are spared in this form

A. Leonine facies + madarosis + many nodules = lepromatous leprosy (no CMI). B describes TT. M. leprae cannot be cultured in vitro; LL has the MOST nerve involvement.

Skin color and pigment disorders MUST KNOW 2027 #70

Depigmented (chalk-white, no melanocytes) = vitiligo → check THYROID and DM. Hypopigmented scaly = pityriasis versicolor or leprosy.

ClueThinkKey point
Chalk-white, sharply marginated, KoebnerVitiligo (depigmented)Autoimmune; no melanocytes. Assoc: thyroid (Hashimoto, Graves) → TFT, DM
Hypopigmented scaly patches, neck/chest/back, humid weather ("an-an")Pityriasis versicolorMalassezia → dicarboxylic acid → inhibits tyrosinase. Not contagious
≥ 6 tan macules > 5 mm (pre-) / > 15 mm (post-puberty)NF1 (CALMs)Normal melanocyte number, more melanin
Dark palmar creases, sun/pressure sites, salt-wastingAddison's↑ ACTH → MC1R
Yellow skin, sclera spared, face then palms/solesCarotenemiaCarotene > 250 mcg/dL; not liver disease; reversible
Yellow skin + yellow scleraJaundiceBilirubin > 3 mg/dL; sclera = best site
Bronze skin + cirrhosisHemochromatosisHFE; ~70%
Blue-gray, sun-exposed, antiarrhythmicAmiodaroneClofazimine (leprosy MDT) = orange-pink; minocycline > 100 mg/d
  • Skin turgor: best site = sternum (wrist loses elasticity with age). Slow return = dehydration.
  • Tyndall effect: dermal melanin looks blue-gray (Mongolian spot, blue nevus).

A 4/F has yellow-orange palms, soles and nasolabial folds. Her mother feeds her mashed squash and carrots daily. The sclerae are white and she is active and well. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

  1. Obstructive jaundice; request liver ultrasound
  2. Hemolytic jaundice; total bilirubin is likely > 3 mg/dL
  3. Addison's disease from ACTH excess
  4. Carotenemia, which spares the sclera and is not a sign of liver disease

D. Look at the sclera: spared = carotenemia (diet, mashed foods ↑ carotene). Jaundice stains the sclera.

Alopecia: type from the clue HIGH-YIELD 2028 #58, #59 2027 #65

Exclamation-mark hairs = alopecia areata. Carpet-tack plugs + lost follicular openings = discoid lupus (scarring, permanent).

TypeScarring?ClueOutcome
Alopecia areataNoRound/oval coin-like bald patches, normal skin, exclamation-mark hairs at margins (distal end broader); fine nail pitting ("hammered brass"); autoimmune thyroidRegrows (stem cell spared); poor if extensive or childhood onset
AndrogeneticNoMost common; miniaturization. Male frontotemporal + vertex (Hamilton); female later, milder (Ludwig)Progressive
Telogen effluviumNoAfter fever, surgery, weight loss; postpartum (3–5 mo after delivery); hair pull (50–60 hairs) = all telogen/club bulbsComplete regrowth
Anagen effluviumNoChemo, radiation, thallium/mercury, protein malnutrition; rapid diffuse loss; tapered fracturesRegrows after chemo
Discoid lupus (cicatricial)YesF > M; scaly erythematous plaques face/scalp/ears; carpet tacks; follicular orifices effacedIrreversible; 1–5% → SLE
  • AA variants: totalis = all scalp hair; universalis = all scalp + body; ophiasis = band along scalp periphery.
  • Hair cycle: anagen 3–5 y (85–90%) · catagen ~2 wk (~1%) · telogen 3–5 mo (club hairs).
  • Hirsutism = women, androgen sites (PCOS) vs hypertrichosis = non-androgen sites (minoxidil, cyclosporine, phenytoin). Acquired lanugo ("malignant down") = internal malignancy.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: coin-shaped bald patch + exclamation hairs (2027, 2028); lupus features + hair loss → cicatricial (2028 #59).
  • Trap: "moth-eaten" alopecia = secondary syphilis (2028 key; not in 2026 trans). Telogen (postpartum, fever) vs anagen (chemo).

A 34/F has scaly, red, round plaques on the cheeks, ears and scalp. Under a lens, the scale's undersurface shows spines like carpet tacks. The bald areas of the scalp are smooth with no visible follicular openings. Which statement is TRUE?

  1. This is alopecia areata, and regrowth is expected
  2. Hair pull test will show all telogen bulbs
  3. This is a scarring alopecia, and the hair loss is irreversible
  4. This is anagen effluvium from autoimmune attack on the matrix

C. DLE destroys follicle stem cells → fibrosis → permanent. Visible follicular openings would mean non-scarring (AA).

Nail changes → disease HIGH-YIELD 2028 #60 2027 #68, #73–74

Half-and-half = kidney (CKD, dialysis). Terry = liver. Spoon = iron deficiency. Clubbing = heart/lung/GI. Pitting + oil spots + onycholysis = psoriasis.

Nail signLookDisease
PittingSmall shallow depressionsPsoriasis (most frequent). Fine "hammered brass" pitting = alopecia areata
Oil spotsSalmon/yellow-brown spots under platePsoriasis (pathognomonic)
OnycholysisPlate separates from distal bedPsoriasis
KoilonychiaSpoon-shaped, concaveIron deficiency anemia, Plummer-Vinson
ClubbingAngle > 180°, bulbous, "rockable"CV (congenital heart disease), pulmonary (CA, suppurative), GI (IBD), methemoglobinemia
Half-and-halfProximal half white, distal pink/brownChronic renal insufficiency, hemodialysis

Beau linesTransverse groove parallel to lunulaShort arrest: high fever, chemo cycles, zinc deficiency
OnychomadesisProximal separation, nail may shedLonger arrest: after hand-foot-mouth disease
Acute paronychiaPainful red swollen fold ± pusS. aureus
  • Fingernail 0.1 mm/day (4–6 mo to replace); big toenail 12–18 mo.

  • Asked as: CKD patient → which nail; nail photo → associated disease; "which nail change is seen in psoriasis" (onycholysis).
  • Trap: half-and-half vs Terry → how much is white: half = kidney; nearly all = liver.

Which nail finding–condition pair is INCORRECT?

  1. Koilonychia – iron deficiency anemia
  2. Terry nails – chronic renal insufficiency on hemodialysis
  3. Onychomadesis – recent hand-foot-mouth disease
  4. Clubbing – cyanotic congenital heart disease

B. Terry nails = severe liver disease. CKD/dialysis = half-and-half nails.

Practice drill — Dr. Yang style

A 45/M has painful, grouped, clear fluid-filled lesions on an erythematous base in a band on the left side of the trunk (T10). Each lesion measures 2–4 mm. What is the primary lesion?

  1. Bullae
  2. Vesicles
  3. Pustules
  4. Papules

B. Fluid-filled and < 1 cm = vesicle (zoster, herpetiform, dermatomal). Clear fluid, not pus.

Same patient, 3 days later: several lesions have merged into tense, clear fluid-filled blisters measuring 1.5 cm. How should these new lesions be described?

  1. Bullae
  2. Vesicles
  3. Wheals
  4. Erosions

A. Fluid-filled ≥ 1 cm = bulla. Same disease, only the size changed (the 2028 trick).

A 9/F with dengue has many grouped, flat, red, 2-mm dots on the legs that do not fade when pressed with a glass slide. What are these lesions?

  1. Purpura
  2. Erythematous macules
  3. Telangiectasia
  4. Petechiae

D. Non-blanching and < 0.5 cm = petechiae. Purpura is ≥ 0.5 cm; erythema would blanch.

The lesion shown is on the leg of a 70/M with poor circulation. Which statement correctly describes it?

  1. An erosion: loss of epidermis only, heals without scar
  2. A fissure: linear crack from decreased elasticity
  3. An ulcer: defect into the dermis or deeper, heals with a scar
  4. A crust: dried serum and blood on the surface

C. Deep crater = ulcer (trans example: leg ulcer). An erosion is shallow and moist and leaves no scar.

A 5/M has the lesions shown on the chin, which started as small blisters. What does the golden-yellow material on top represent, and what is the likely diagnosis?

  1. Crust (dried exudate) – impetigo
  2. Scales (stratum corneum) – psoriasis
  3. Lichenification – atopic dermatitis
  4. Pustules – acne vulgaris

A. 📌 Honey-colored crust = impetigo (trans sample case 3). Crust is dried serum/pus/blood, a secondary lesion.

Identify the primary lesion shown.

  1. Vesicles
  2. Pustules
  3. Nodules
  4. Wheals

B. Raised lesions with visible white-yellow pus = pustules (any size). Vesicles contain clear/serous fluid.

A 20/M basketball player has the lesions shown on the upper back, worse in hot humid months. They are hypopigmented, oval, coalescing, with fine scales. Which bedside finding is expected?

  1. KOH: long, narrow, septate, branching hyphae without constriction
  2. Wood's lamp: coral-red fluorescence
  3. KOH: short hyphae and yeast forms ("ziti and meatballs"); Wood's lamp yellow-green
  4. Tzanck: multinucleated giant cells

C. Pityriasis versicolor (trans case 6). A = dermatophyte; B = erythrasma.

These nails (almost entirely white and opaque, with only a narrow pink band at the tip) were seen in a 58/M. Which condition should you look for?

  1. Iron deficiency anemia
  2. Chronic renal insufficiency
  3. Psoriasis
  4. Severe liver disease

D. Terry nails = liver. Half-and-half (proximal half white, distal half pink/brown) = kidney (near-miss).

A 50/F has flaccid blisters on the trunk and painful oral erosions for 2 months, with no new medications. When the examiner presses straight down on an intact blister, the blister extends into the surrounding skin. Which sign is this, and where is the split?

  1. Nikolsky sign; subepidermal
  2. Asboe-Hansen sign; above the basement membrane (suprabasal)
  3. Darier sign; dermal mast cells
  4. Auspitz sign; papillary dermis

B. Downward pressure on an existing bulla = Asboe-Hansen. Positive in PV (suprabasal acantholysis). Nikolsky uses lateral pressure on unblistered skin.

Which test or sign and its finding is INCORRECTLY matched?

  1. Wood's lamp coral-red fluorescence – pityriasis versicolor
  2. Diascopy apple-jelly sign – sarcoidosis
  3. Tzanck smear multinucleated giant cells – herpes zoster
  4. Darier sign – urticaria pigmentosa

A. Coral red = erythrasma (Corynebacterium). Pityriasis versicolor gives yellow-green.

A 29/F gave birth 4 months ago and now notices large amounts of hair on her pillow and comb, all over the scalp. No bald patches or scalp inflammation are seen. A hair pull test yields hairs with depigmented, rounded club ends. What is the diagnosis?

  1. Alopecia areata
  2. Anagen effluvium
  3. Telogen effluvium
  4. Androgenetic alopecia

C. Postpartum synchronous shedding of telogen (club) hairs at 3–5 months; full regrowth. Anagen effluvium follows chemo/toxins.

A 40/M from an endemic area has a few well-defined, hypopigmented plaques with raised edges on one arm. Which finding on sensitivity evaluation of the lesions would SUPPORT your suspected diagnosis?

  1. Increased sweating on the iodine-starch test
  2. Intense pruritus on stroking
  3. Hyperalgesia to the tip of a needle
  4. Inability to feel a cotton wisp

D. Tuberculoid leprosy: hypesthetic/anesthetic lesions (nerves already damaged), with reduced, not increased, sweating.

A 3/M has many tan-brown macules and papules on the trunk. Rubbing one lesion with a pen end produces a wheal limited to that lesion after a few minutes. He needs pain relief after a minor fracture. Which of the following is a mast-cell degranulator that must be AVOIDED?

  1. Codeine
  2. Paracetamol
  3. Cetirizine
  4. Plain normal saline

A. (+) Darier = urticaria pigmentosa (mastocytosis). 📌 Avoid degranulators: codeine, morphine, aspirin/NSAIDs, alcohol, etc.; children can go into shock.

A 62/M on long-term hemodialysis is referred for skin and nail changes. Which nail finding is MOST expected?

  1. Spoon-shaped concave nails
  2. Proximal half whitish, distal half pinkish-brown
  3. Salmon-colored oil spots
  4. Swollen, tender, pus-filled lateral nail fold

B. Half-and-half nails = chronic renal insufficiency/hemodialysis. A = iron deficiency; C = psoriasis; D = paronychia (S. aureus).

A 27/F has depigmented, chalk-white, sharply marginated patches around the mouth and on the fingertips that also appeared on a recent scratch. Diascopy and KOH are negative. Which work-up is MOST appropriate?

  1. Patch test for allergic contact dermatitis
  2. Slit-skin smear for acid-fast bacilli
  3. Thyroid function tests and blood sugar
  4. Serum carotene level

C. Depigmented (chalk-white) + Koebner + lip-tip pattern = vitiligo → check thyroid (Hashimoto, Graves) and DM. Leprosy lesions are hypopigmented, not chalk-white.

Last-look cram sheet

  • 1 cm: macule/patch, papule/plaque-nodule, vesicle/bulla. > 5 cm tumor. 0.5 cm petechiae/purpura. Wheal & pustule: no cutoff.
  • 3 mm fluid = vesicle; 3 cm fluid = bulla. READ THE UNIT.
  • Wheal = gone in 24–48 h. Nodule = domed, deep. Plaque = plateau. Pustule = pus.
  • Honey-colored crust → impetigo 📌. Silvery scales → psoriasis. Thick lined skin → lichenification (rubbing). Linear scratches → excoriation. Sole cracks → fissure.
  • Erosion = epidermis, no scar. Ulcer = dermis, scar. Keloid = scar beyond wound.
  • OTC clobetasol cream → atrophy (cigarette-paper), irreversible.
  • Diascopy: erythema blanches; purpura, petechiae, telangiectasia don't. Apple-jelly → sarcoidosis.
  • Derm PE BEFORE history 📌. Primary lesion = main diagnostic basis. Order: N-A-M-C-S-P-S-L.
  • Palms/soles copper-colored → sexual history (syphilis). Linear → plants. Herpetiform → herpes. Umbilicated → molluscum. Target → EM. Palm = 1% BSA.
  • Nikolsky (intact skin, lateral) and Asboe-Hansen (on bulla, downward) → PV, TEN. Negative Nikolsky = subepidermal.
  • TEN: drug 4–28 days; SJS < 10%, overlap 10–30%, TEN > 30%.
  • Auspitz → psoriasis (not specific). Darier → mastocytosis (avoid opioids, aspirin/NSAIDs, alcohol 📌). Dimple → dermatofibroma.
  • Wood's: coral red erythrasma; yellow-green PV; green-yellow Microsporum; T. tonsurans NO glow 📌.
  • KOH: septate branching hyphae = tinea; pseudohyphae + buds = Candida; ziti/spaghetti and meatballs = PV. Tzanck: multinucleated giant cells = herpes. Patch test: ACD, read 48 h, final 72/96 h.
  • Leprosy → test sensation (cotton, needle, temperature, iodine-starch); lesions anesthetic, anhidrotic. TT good CMI; LL no CMI, leonine facies, madarosis.
  • Vitiligo → thyroid + DM. Yellow skin + white sclera → carotenemia. Turgor → sternum. ≥ 6 CALMs → NF1.
  • Exclamation-mark hairs → alopecia areata (regrows). Carpet tacks → DLE (scarring, permanent). Postpartum/fever → telogen effluvium. Chemo → anagen effluvium.
  • Nails: pitting (most frequent) + oil spots (pathognomonic) + onycholysis → psoriasis. Half-and-half → CKD. Terry → liver. Spoon → iron deficiency. Clubbing → heart/lung/GI. Beau lines → arrest (chemo, fever). Onychomadesis → HFMD.

2.03 Approach to Malignancy; Cancer Screening & Prevention 19 items

Dr. Arthur Jason Go (NEW, no past exam from him) · Recall 4 / Comp 5 / App 4 / Analysis 6 · Past-exam style source: none. The 2027/2028 items were written by a different professor, so use them for TOPICS only and follow the 2026 trans.

How Dr. Go will likely ask
  • His trans follows one frame: Diagnosis → Stage → Plan → Support (he underlined it). Expect "next best step" cases: tissue before treatment, staging before the plan, fix reversible causes before calling the patient "too frail".
  • Prevention part: which level (primary/secondary/tertiary), which agent (chemo-, immuno-, surgical prevention) and its harm, and who qualifies for which screening (PHEX ages, intervals, tests).
  • Trans cases he wrote himself: the "complete cancer blood test" smoker (answer: address tobacco first), the screen-found lung nodule (follow a standard pathway), the ECOG 3 lymphoma patient with hypercalcemia (reversible), and the new breast mass (mammogram + biopsy → CT → plan).
  • Numbers he may test: RECIST 30% / WHO >50% / progression 20%, pain 70-20-10, nausea timing, nutrition cut-offs, PHEX intervals.
Past-exam concept map (2027 / 2028) — different professor, topics only
Concept20282027Covered in
First / priority step in the cancer patient#19, #28#23, #28Framework, Diagnosis
TNM, stage = best prognostic factor#20, #21—Staging
Role of a CT after treatment (surveillance vs staging)—#24Staging
Performance status: why, which scale, ECOG matching#25, #35#36–38ECOG vs Karnofsky
Tumor markers (CA-125, CEA, AFP, CD30)—#20, #33–35Tumor markers
Cancer pain (most common cause)#29#30Supportive care
Chemo side effect / cachexia#23, #24—Supportive care

Smoking cessation 30–50%—#32Prevention levels
