Purpose of screening, lead-time bias#26, #33#21 (sensitivity)Screening biases
Low-dose CT eligibility (repeated)#30#22, #29LDCT
Mammogram age / breast screening (repeated)#27#25, #29PHEX table
Spinal cord compression (emergency)—#27Emergencies (Harrison's)

The 4-step frame: Diagnosis → Stage → Plan → Support HIGH-YIELD LECTURER 2028 #19, #28 2027 #23, #28

Always go in this order: (1) establish the diagnosis, (2) find the extent (stage), (3) make a treatment plan, (4) manage disease and treatment complications.

  • No treatment before tissue proof. No plan before staging.
  • Step 2 also covers physiologic reserve (performance status) and tumor biology.
  • Step 3 needs an explicit goal: curative or palliative.
  • Step 4 = supportive care, response assessment, end-of-life care.
  • He closes the lecture with "Diagnosis, stage, plan, support" (underlined). p. 1, 3
TRAP: "priority once cancer is established" Both the 2027 (#28) and 2028 (#28) keys chose "disclosure of diagnosis to the patient", over "extent of disease" and "treatment plan". The current trans does not list disclosure as a step, but it does stress truthful communication. If the stem says the diagnosis is already established and "disclosure" is a choice, that was the old key. If disclosure is not a choice, pick the next framework step (extent/staging).
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "newly diagnosed via biopsy… next step?", "a mass is seen on imaging… next step?"
  • Trap: "start chemo" or "PET-CT" before tissue → how to tell: ask "do we have a biopsy yet?" If no, biopsy. If yes, stage.

A 61/M had a core-needle biopsy of a colonic mass showing adenocarcinoma. His physician now orders a CT of the chest and abdomen to look for liver and lung lesions. In the approach to the cancer patient, this CT belongs to which step?

  1. Establishing the diagnosis
  2. Determining the extent of disease
  3. Making the treatment plan
  4. Managing treatment complications

B. The diagnosis is already proven by tissue. Looking for spread = staging (extent). The plan comes after.

Step 1: Diagnosis needs tissue; Cancer of Unknown Primary MUST KNOW

Invasive tissue biopsy is the starting point. Imaging or a tumor marker alone does not diagnose cancer.

  • FNAB (fine-needle aspiration biopsy) is used for thyroid cancer.
  • CUP (metastasis found, primary unknown): detailed history + focused search + biopsy the nearest accessible tissue.
  • On the tissue: IHC (immunohistochemistry) is his example of tumor-marker use; consider gene expression testing / NGS for driver mutations.
  • NGS is predictive (tells if a targeted drug will work), not only prognostic (underlined).
  • Multidisciplinary team improves decision quality (colon → GI, lung → pulmonologist). p. 1–2
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: lymph node or liver mass with no obvious primary; "elevated marker, start treatment?"
  • Trap: whole-body PET-CT or "repeat tumor markers" → how to tell: the trans says biopsy the nearest accessible tissue.

A 66/F has a hard, fixed 3 cm left supraclavicular lymph node. Breast, pelvic and skin exams are unremarkable, and she has no localizing symptoms. Which is the most appropriate next step?

  1. Start empiric chemotherapy for a presumed lung primary
  2. Request CEA, CA-125 and AFP to identify the primary
  3. Observe and repeat the exam in 3 months
  4. Biopsy the lymph node, with IHC on the tissue, after a detailed history

D. CUP: history, focused search, biopsy the nearest accessible tissue. Markers rarely diagnose (B), and no treatment is given without tissue (A).

Step 2: Staging systems and TNM HIGH-YIELD 2028 #20, #21 2027 #24

Outcome depends on 3 things: extent of disease, physiologic reserve, tumor biology. TNM (AJCC) is the most common staging system.

Clinical stagingPathologic staging
Based onExam, imaging, other pre-treatment infoOperative and tissue findings
Tells youEarly vs advanced; function good vs badTumor biology (how aggressive)
MemoryBefore the knifeAfter the knife
SystemUsed for
TNM (AJCC)Most cancers. T = tumor (size or depth), N = nodes, M = distant metastasis
Ann ArborHodgkin's lymphoma
DukesColorectal (but TNM is still used in practice)
FIGOGynecologic cancers
  • T by size for breast; T by depth of penetration for colorectal and uterine. p. 1
Past-exam extra (not in the 2026 trans): surveillance = scans after finished treatment to look for recurrence (2027 #24); staging = at first diagnosis; screening = asymptomatic people without the disease.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: system-to-cancer matching; clinical vs pathologic stage; how T is graded.
  • Trap: Dukes for colorectal is "correct" as a name, but TNM is still what is used.

Which staging system and cancer pairing is INCORRECT?

  1. Ann Arbor — Hodgkin's lymphoma
  2. Dukes — colorectal cancer
  3. FIGO — non-Hodgkin lymphoma
  4. TNM — most solid tumors

C. FIGO is for gynecologic cancers. Lymphoma uses Ann Arbor.

Performance status: ECOG vs Karnofsky; poor PS may be reversible HIGH-YIELD LECTURER 2028 #25, #35 2027 #36–38

Performance status estimates physiologic reserve, which tells you whether the patient can tolerate treatment. Karnofsky counts up to health (100 = normal); ECOG counts up to death (5 = dead).

ECOGMeaningKarnofsky (trans anchors)
0Fully active100 normal, no complaints
1Restricted to light work—
2Ambulatory, self-care, cannot work70 self-care, unable to work
3Limited self-care, bed/chair >50% of waking hours50 needs considerable assistance
4No self-care, completely disabled—
5Dead0 dead

The trans aligns rows by direction only and gives no exact KPS-to-ECOG conversion. p. 1

  • ECOG 3–4 at baseline = limited treatment options (lecturer).
  • Exception: if the cancer itself causes the poor PS and the patient can respond, treating may still be warranted.
  • Trans case: 58/F, new lymphoma, ECOG 3, hypercalcemia, dehydration, severe pain → treat the reversible problems, clarify baseline function, reassess after stabilizing.
  • "PS is a clinical finding, not a verdict" (underlined). p. 2
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: describe a patient's day → pick the score; "why assess PS?" (to know if the patient can tolerate treatment).
  • Trap: ECOG 2 vs 3 → how to tell: up and about more than half the day = 2; in bed/chair more than half = 3. And PS does not measure extent of disease.

A 70/M with prostate cancer can no longer care for himself without frequent help and needs regular medical care, but he is not bedridden all day. Which Karnofsky score from the lecture best fits?

  1. 50
  2. 70
  3. 100
  4. 0

A. KPS 50 = considerable assistance. KPS 70 is still independent in self-care (only unable to work).

Tumor markers monitor, they rarely diagnose MUST KNOW 2027 #20, #33–35

Use markers after the diagnosis: for a baseline, to follow response, and to raise concern for recurrence. Not for diagnosis, and not for screening the "complete cancer blood test" patient.

MarkerCancerBenign causes (trap)
AFPHCC, gonadal germ-cell tumorCirrhosis, hepatitis
CEAAdenocarcinomas: colon, pancreas, lung, breast, ovaryPancreatitis, hepatitis, IBD, smoking
CA-125Ovarian, some lymphomasMenstruation, pregnancy, peritonitis
PSAProstateProstatitis, BPH
  • A marker can be normal despite cancer (colon cancer with normal CEA).
  • Uses: baseline (pre-op CEA), response (stage 4 colon CEA 50 → falling), recurrence (rising in an adjuvant patient), and they complement, not replace, imaging.
  • Pitfalls: benign elevation, not every tumor secretes one, assay/timing variation. Never treat a number alone. p. 2
Old keys used Harrison's markers not in this trans: CD30 → Hodgkin's / anaplastic large-cell lymphoma, CD25 → hairy-cell leukemia, CA 19-9 → pancreas/colon. Harrison's
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: elevated marker in a patient with a benign condition; "appropriate use of a marker".
  • Trap: "elevated CEA → diagnose colon cancer". Markers support decisions only once tissue has proven the cancer.

Each of the following can raise CA-125 without cancer, EXCEPT:

  1. Menstruation
  2. Pregnancy
  3. Smoking
  4. Peritonitis

C. In the trans, smoking is a benign cause of a high CEA. Menses, pregnancy and peritonitis are the CA-125 list.

Step 3–4: Curative vs palliative intent; response criteria MUST KNOW

The goal must be stated. Early stage → curative. Advanced stage → palliative. Response is measured with objective, repeatable tools (RECIST, markers).

CurativePalliative
StageEarlyAdvanced
ToxicityAccepts short-term toxicity for cureLow tolerance; aggressive chemo not recommended
DeliveryPrecise protocol, combined modalities (surgery + RT)Symptom and disease control, comfort, continuity
GoalCure, definitive assessmentQuality and duration of life
ResponseDefinition
CompleteAll disease gone (10 → 0)
Partial≥30% decrease (RECIST) or >50% (WHO) in summed diameters
Progressive20% increase or any new lesion
StableNeither
  • Any new symptom during treatment = reversible until proven otherwise. p. 2
Solved example Masses 4 + 3 + 3 cm = 10. After 2 cycles: 2 + 2 + 3 = 7.
  1. (10 − 7) ÷ 10 = 0.30 → 30% decrease
  2. RECIST: ≥30% → partial response
  3. WHO: needs >50% → not met
  4. Any new lesion, even if the sum fell → progressive
Shortcut / trap Sum only the original lesions; a new lesion is progression by itself. Do not swap 30 / 50 / 20.

Which feature belongs to a PALLIATIVE treatment plan?

  1. Accepts short-term toxicity in exchange for cure
  2. Lower tolerance for toxicity, with focus on symptom control
  3. Combined surgery and radiotherapy delivered by a precise protocol
  4. Plans a definitive assessment of cure

B. A, C and D are curative-intent features.

Supportive and end-of-life care: pain, nausea, depression, nutrition HIGH-YIELD 2028 #23, #29 2027 #30

Treat the person, not just the tumor. Cancer pain is mostly from the tumor itself (70%).

TopicTrans numbers
Pain causes70% tumor · 20% treatment · 10% other
Nausea timingAcute <24 h · Delayed 1–7 d · Anticipatory = before chemo is given
Highly emetogenic prophylaxisOndansetron 8 mg PO q6h the day before + IV on the day; dexamethasone 20 mg IV; aprepitant 125 mg d1 → 80 mg d2–3
Depression~25%; screen ≥2 wk low mood/anhedonia; SSRI or TCA; wait 4–6 wk
Nutrition triggers>10% weight loss, transferrin <150 mg/dL, albumin <3.4 g/dL → enteral over parenteral; megestrol may help
End of lifeInfection = #1 cause of death in cancer patients; ~70% preterminal dyspnea; be truthful, promise no abandonment
TRAP: "most common side effect/complication of therapy" 2028 #23 keyed nausea/vomiting as the most common chemo side effect. The trans review-question key says the most common complication of cancer therapy is myelosuppression (answer key only, not in the lecture body). Read the wording: "complication of therapy" → myelosuppression. 2028 #24 (cachexia from tumor metabolic effects) came from Harrison's.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: timing story → nausea type; lab values → start nutrition support.
  • Trap: anticipatory vs acute → how to tell: anticipatory begins before the drug is given.

A 45/F on her fourth cycle of cisplatin starts vomiting in the clinic waiting room while waiting for the infusion to be hung. Which type of chemotherapy-related nausea is this?

  1. Acute
  2. Delayed
  3. Breakthrough from the previous dose
  4. Anticipatory

D. No drug has been given yet. Acute = within 24 h after; delayed = days 1–7 after.

Malignant effusions: step-up management 2027 #31

Pleural: thoracentesis → chest tube (if symptomatic recurrence within 2 weeks) → pleurodesis. Pericardial tamponade → window. Ascites → small-volume paracentesis.

  • Lung, breast, lymphoma = 75% of malignant effusions.
  • Asymptomatic effusion may need no treatment. If symptomatic, first weigh systemic-therapy response and expected survival.
  • Pericardial: window (tamponade), stripping, chemical sclerosis. Ascites: paracentesis, selected shunts. p. 2
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: metastatic breast/lung cancer, effusion, relief after tap, dyspnea returns in under 2 weeks → ?
  • Trap: "repeat thoracentesis" → recurrence within 2 weeks calls for a chest tube, then pleurodesis.

A 59/M with stage IV lung cancer has hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds; echo shows a large pericardial effusion with tamponade. Per the trans, which site-specific palliation fits?

  1. Pericardial window
  2. Pleurodesis
  3. Small-volume paracentesis
  4. Observation, since malignant effusions may not need treatment

A. Tamponade → window. "No treatment" applies only to asymptomatic effusions.

Levels of prevention, carcinogenesis steps, tobacco first HIGH-YIELD LECTURER 2027 #32

Primary = no cancer yet (change exposures). Secondary = screening asymptomatic people. Tertiary = treating symptomatic cancer. Tobacco cessation is the highest-yield prevention action.

Carcinogenesis stepWhat interrupts itLevel
1 Initiation (DNA/epigenetic injury)Exercise, stop smoking, sun avoidancePrimary
2 Promotion (growth signals)VaccinationPrimary
3 Progression (invasion)ScreeningSecondary
  • ~1 in 3 smokers die early; smoking shortens life by ~10 years.
  • Quitting → 30–50% lower 10-year lung-cancer mortality, even after mutations exist.
  • Ask everyone (incl. vaping) · Advise complete cessation (not "light" cigarettes) · Assist with counseling + pharmacotherapy.
  • Cigars and smokeless tobacco are not safe substitutes; secondhand smoke is carcinogenic; prevention starts in adolescence. p. 3
His Case 1 52/M, 20 cigarettes/day, BMI 31, sedentary, asks for a "complete cancer blood test" → address tobacco use first. Avoid tumor markers, whole-body CT and MCED. "Prevention earns priority. Screening earns scrutiny." p. 3, 5

Which of the following is an example of SECONDARY cancer prevention?

  1. HPV vaccination of a 12-year-old girl
  2. Chest tube and pleurodesis for a malignant effusion
  3. Annual FIT in an asymptomatic 55-year-old
  4. Smoking-cessation counseling for a 30-year-old smoker

C. Screening asymptomatic people = secondary. A and D are primary; B treats symptomatic cancer (tertiary).

Carcinogens and lifestyle evidence 2028 #34

Know the exposure → cancer pairs. Lifestyle advice is strongest when it has broad health benefits.

CarcinogenCancers
TobaccoUpper aerodigestive, lung, bladder, kidney
AsbestosLung, pleura (mesothelioma), peritoneum
AlcoholBreast, liver, esophagus, head and neck
UV radiationSkin; lecturer: more SCC than melanoma (actinic keratosis → SCC)
Aromatic aminesBladder
Ionizing radiationMultiple solid + hematologic
  • Physical activity → lower colon and breast cancer. Higher BMI → modestly more cancers.
  • Low-fat/high-fiber trials did not clearly reduce cancer; supplements have no established anticancer value. p. 3
  • Old-key extras: benzene → leukemia (2028 #34); schistosomiasis → squamous bladder cancer (trans review key). Harrison's

A 58/M who worked 25 years in a dye factory presents with painless gross hematuria. Which carcinogen and cancer pair is most likely?

  1. Asbestos — mesothelioma
  2. Aromatic amines — bladder cancer
  3. Alcohol — kidney cancer
  4. UV radiation — squamous cell carcinoma

B. Aromatic amines (dye industry) → bladder. Kidney is on the tobacco list, not alcohol.

Chemoprevention: benefit must beat harm LECTURER

Chemoprevention = a natural or synthetic agent given BEFORE invasive cancer to reverse, suppress or prevent carcinogenesis (underlined). A plausible agent can still cause net harm.

AgentEffectHarm / lesson
Beta caroteneLooked protective in observational dataRCTs in smokers: MORE lung cancer. Plausibility ≠ outcome
Aspirin↓ adenomas and CRC after long follow-upBleeding; net benefit depends on age, CV and bleeding risk
Tamoxifen (SERM)↓ ER-positive breast cancerVTE, endometrial cancer, cataracts, hot flashes
Raloxifene (SERM)↓ invasive breast cancer, postmenopausalLess uterine toxicity, still VTE
Aromatase inhibitorsLarge relative reductionMusculoskeletal symptoms, osteoporosis
Finasteride~25% fewer prostate cancers diagnosedMore high-grade cancers, alters PSA; not FDA-approved for prevention
  • Mechanisms: antimutagenic, hormonal, anti-inflammatory, antiproliferative/proapoptotic.
  • Breast chemoprevention: confirm high risk by history first, then individualized risk estimate + shared decision-making. p. 3

A 50/F heavy smoker read that carrots "fight cancer" and asks to start high-dose beta-carotene supplements to prevent lung cancer. Best advice?

  1. Discourage it: randomized trials in smokers showed more lung cancer
  2. Encourage it: observational studies showed lower lung cancer rates
  3. Allow it only with yearly chest X-ray screening
  4. Recommend aspirin instead, which prevents lung cancer

A. The beta-carotene lesson: do not trust plausibility over outcomes. Aspirin's evidence is for colorectal cancer.

Immunoprevention (vaccines) and surgical prevention 2028 #31

Vaccines prevent cancers caused by chronic infection. Surgery is powerful but irreversible, and some risk remains afterwards.

TypeIntervention → cancer prevented
ImmunoHBV vaccine → hepatocellular carcinoma
ImmunoHPV vaccine (16, 18) → cervical, oropharyngeal
Infection controlH. pylori eradication → gastric adenocarcinoma (selected settings)
SurgicalProphylactic mastectomy; salpingo-oophorectomy (hereditary breast-ovarian, BRCA)
SurgicalColectomy in FAP
  • Weigh: true inherited risk, residual risk, fertility/endocrine/sexual/psychosocial effects.
  • Lecture example: Angelina Jolie (BRCA1) → bilateral mastectomy + oophorectomy (removes estrogen source). p. 3–4

A 22/M has hundreds of colonic adenomas and an APC mutation (familial adenomatous polyposis). Which cancer-preventive strategy from the lecture applies?

  1. Finasteride chemoprevention
  2. HBV vaccination
  3. Prophylactic colectomy
  4. Annual FIT starting at age 50

C. FAP → colectomy (surgical prevention). Population FIT screening does not fit a hereditary near-certain risk.

Screening is a program; screening biases HIGH-YIELD 2028 #26, #33

Judge screening by lower disease-specific mortality, not by longer survival after diagnosis. Longer survival can be an artifact of bias.

Lead-time biasLength biasOverdiagnosisSelection (volunteer) bias Harrison's — not in 2.03 trans
What happensDiagnosed earlier, dies at the same timeSlow tumors stay detectable longerCancer that would never have caused harmPeople who volunteer for screening are healthier to begin with
EffectLonger measured survival, no longer lifeScreening finds favorable disease; fast ones missedMore diagnosis and treatment, no benefitScreened group looks better for reasons unrelated to screening
MemoryThe clock started earlierSlowNeverWho signed up
  • Program chain: eligible asymptomatic population → accurate acceptable test → timely confirmation → effective earlier treatment. Benefit can fail at any link.
  • Harms: false positives + invasive work-up, false reassurance (false negatives), overdiagnosis/overtreatment, radiation, anxiety, cost. p. 4
  • Test terms (from 2.01): sensitivity = with disease and test positive (2027 #21).
TRAP 2028 #26 keyed "diagnose at an early stage" as the purpose of screening. The current trans adds that early detection only counts if it lowers mortality/morbidity. If both are choices, "reduce disease-specific mortality" is the trans answer.

In a new screening program, the tumors found by the screening test are mostly low-grade and slow-growing, while aggressive cancers keep appearing between screening rounds. This pattern illustrates:

  1. Lead-time bias
  2. Length bias
  3. Overdiagnosis
  4. False-negative reassurance

B. Slow tumors stay detectable longer, so screening finds them; fast ones show up as interval cancers. Overdiagnosis = cancers that would never matter.

Who gets screened for what: PHEX adult recommendations HIGH-YIELD MUST KNOW 2028 #27 2027 #25, #29

Mortality evidence exists for 4 cancers (CBCL): Cervical, Breast, Colorectal, Lung. In PHEX, everything is green (recommended) except prostate (blue = shared decision-making).

CancerWhoTest · interval
CervicalWomen 30–65Cytology q3y OR high-risk HPV test q5y (VIA q3y alternative)
BreastWomen 50–69Mammography q1–2y; yearly if family history or BRCA
BreastWomen ≥50Clinical breast exam q2y
ColonAdults 50+ (PH; 45–50 abroad)FOBT/FIT yearly; positive → colonoscopy. Sigmoidoscopy q5y, colonoscopy q10y if normal
LungHigh risk, 50–80, >20 pack-yearsAnnual low-dose CT
LiverAt risk for HCC, ± cirrhosisUltrasound + AFP q6 months
NasopharyngealFirst-degree relative with NPCEBV DNA and/or nasopharyngoscopy
Prostate (blue)Asymptomatic men 50–64Shared decision before biennial PSA + DRE
  • Breast MRI: only for selected high-risk, younger patients, not population screening.
  • Controversial: ovarian CA-125 + TVUS (no mortality benefit, false positives → major surgery); PSA (small/uncertain benefit).
  • MCED blood tests: no demonstrated outcome benefit, not routine. p. 4–5
TRAP: old keys vs current trans 2027 #25 keyed mammography from age 40 (USPSTF/ACS); 2028 #27 keyed 50–74 biennial. The current trans (PHEX) says 50–69, every 1–2 years. 2027 #29 keyed an annual Pap smear; PHEX says cytology every 3 years (or HPV q5y) for ages 30–65. Follow the trans.

A 54/F with no symptoms has a mother who had breast cancer at age 60. She has never been screened. Per the PHEX recommendations in the trans, what breast screening should she get?

  1. Mammography every 2 years
  2. Annual breast MRI alone
  3. Clinical breast exam only, since she is under 70
  4. Yearly mammography

D. Ages 50–69 get mammography q1–2y; family history or BRCA → yearly. MRI is not routine population screening.

Lung screening: low-dose CT eligibility and what happens after HIGH-YIELD 2028 #30 2027 #22, #29

Only low-dose CT (not chest X-ray) lowers lung-cancer mortality, and only in high-risk smokers: age 50–80 with >20 pack-years, yearly.

Formula Pack-years = packs per day × years smoked.
  1. 1.5 packs/day × 18 years = 27 pack-years
  2. Check age 50–80 → check >20 pack-years → able to undergo curative treatment
Shortcut / trap Family history, radon or asbestos alone do not make someone eligible. Chest X-ray screening: no mortality benefit. NLST: ~3 fewer deaths per 1,000 vs CXR.
  • Eligibility = age, smoking exposure, health, and ability to undergo curative treatment.
  • His Case 2: 62-year-old smoker with a small nodule on screening LDCT → estimate malignancy probability, follow a standardized diagnostic pathway, do not dismiss and do not rush to invasive treatment, continue cessation support. p. 4–5
TRAP: changing criteria 2027 #29 rationale used 55–80 with ≥30 pack-years and 2028 #30 keyed "30 pack-years". 2027 #22 used 50–80, ≥20 pack-years, quit within 15 years. The current trans says 50–80, >20 pack-years. The "quit within 15 years" rule is not in the trans.

Which asymptomatic patient qualifies for annual low-dose CT screening per the current trans?

  1. 48/M, 2 packs/day for 20 years
  2. 58/F, half a pack/day for 30 years
  3. 63/M, 1.5 packs/day for 18 years, still smoking
  4. 82/M, 2 packs/day for 40 years

C. 27 pack-years, age 63. A = 40 PY but too young; B = only 15 PY; D = over 80.

Oncologic emergencies (compact) Harrison's — not in 2.03 trans 2027 #27

Past exams included emergency cases, but Dr. Go's trans does not cover them. Learn these 4 one-liners only.

EmergencyClueKey move
Spinal cord compressionKnown cancer (lung, breast, prostate, myeloma) + back pain worse lying flat → leg weakness; thoracic 70%High-dose dexamethasone now → MRI of the whole spine → radiation + steroids (surgery if unstable)
SVC syndromeFacial/neck swelling, dilated chest veins, worse lying down; lung cancer ~85% (young → lymphoma)CT; NSCLC → radiation; SCLC/lymphoma/germ cell → chemo; stent if severe. Danger = tracheal compression
Tumor lysis syndromeBurkitt/ALL, 1–5 days after chemo: ↑uric acid, ↑K, ↑PO4, ↓Ca, AKIPrevent: allopurinol + IV fluids; rasburicase if high risk (never in G6PD deficiency)
HypercalcemiaMost common paraneoplastic syndrome; can make PS look worseCorrect it (and dehydration), then reassess PS (trans case)
  • Neutropenia + infection = most common serious complication of treatment; infection = #1 cause of death in cancer patients (trans).

A 68/M with metastatic prostate cancer has 2 weeks of mid-back pain that is worse at night when lying flat, and today cannot climb stairs because of leg weakness. What should be done FIRST?

  1. Give high-dose dexamethasone, then MRI of the whole spine
  2. Plain X-ray of the thoracic spine, then decide
  3. Start NSAIDs and reassess in 2 weeks as mechanical back pain
  4. EMG/NCV of the lower extremities

A. Suspected cord compression: steroids right away, then MRI. X-rays often miss it, and outcome depends on treating while he can still walk.

Practice drill — Dr. Go style (framework and prevention cases)

A 57/M smoker has a 4 cm right hilar mass on CT and a CEA of 28 ng/mL. His family asks that chemotherapy be started this week. What is the next best step?

  1. Start chemotherapy, since the CEA confirms adenocarcinoma
  2. Repeat CEA in 4 weeks to see the trend
  3. Obtain tissue (biopsy) to establish the diagnosis
  4. Refer to palliative care because of the high CEA

C. Diagnosis starts with tissue. CEA also rises with smoking and never diagnoses cancer on its own.

A 41/F has a right breast mass enlarging over 4 months, unrelated to her cycle. Mammogram and core biopsy show invasive ductal carcinoma. What comes next?

  1. Modified radical mastectomy right away
  2. Determine extent with physical exam and imaging (e.g., CT) before planning treatment
  3. Start tamoxifen chemoprevention
  4. Repeat mammogram in 6 months

B. Trans case: mammogram + biopsy → extent (PE + CT) → plan. Surgery before staging skips a step. Chemoprevention is for people without invasive cancer.

A 63/F with newly diagnosed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma has been bedbound for 10 days with severe bone pain, confusion, serum calcium 13.8 mg/dL and dry mucosa. Her daughter says she was gardening daily a month ago. The resident labels her ECOG 3, "not a candidate for therapy." Best next step?

  1. Agree and refer for hospice only
  2. Give full-dose chemotherapy today regardless of status
  3. Repeat the ECOG score tomorrow without other changes
  4. Correct the hypercalcemia and dehydration, control pain, then reassess performance status

D. PS is a finding, not a verdict: fix reversible causes, clarify baseline (she was active), reassess. Chemo without stabilizing (B) skips the trans step.

A patient with stage IV colon cancer had CEA 50 at diagnosis, which fell to 6 after chemotherapy. On follow-up it is now 34, and he feels well. What is the most appropriate interpretation and action?

  1. Concern for recurrence/progression; confirm with imaging before changing treatment
  2. Diagnostic of progression; switch chemotherapy now
  3. Meaningless, because CEA is not useful after diagnosis
  4. Probably lab error; stop monitoring markers

A. A rising marker raises concern, but markers complement, not replace, imaging. Never treat a number alone (B).

Three liver metastases measured 5, 3 and 2 cm before treatment. After 3 cycles they measure 4, 3 and 2 cm, and a new 1 cm lesion appears in the lung. The response category is:

  1. Partial response
  2. Stable disease
  3. Progressive disease
  4. Complete response

C. Any new lesion = progression, even though the original sum fell from 10 to 9 (only 10%, which would otherwise be stable).

A 36/F asks how often she needs cervical screening. Her co-tested cytology and high-risk HPV test today are both negative. Per PHEX in the trans, when is her next screen?

  1. In 1 year
  2. In 5 years
  3. In 3 years
  4. No further screening needed after one negative HPV test

B. With HPV testing → every 5 years; cytology alone → every 3 years. Annual Pap (an old key) is not the trans interval.

A 52/M, average risk, did a FIT for screening and it came back positive. What is the next step?

  1. Repeat the FIT next year
  2. Serum CEA to decide if work-up is needed
  3. CT colonography as the definitive test
  4. Colonoscopy

D. Any positive stool test (or CT colonography) → colonoscopy. A screening program fails if abnormal results are not followed up.

A 58/M without urinary symptoms asks for a PSA test "to be safe." Per PHEX, what is the most appropriate approach?

  1. Discuss benefits and harms (shared decision-making) before biennial PSA + DRE
  2. Order annual PSA, since it is a green (recommended) test
  3. Refuse; PSA is never used for screening
  4. Order PSA with CA-125 and CEA as a cancer panel

A. Prostate is the only blue (shared decision) row: men 50–64, biennial PSA + DRE after discussing overdiagnosis.

Which screening pairing for an asymptomatic adult is INCORRECT per the trans?

  1. Chronic hepatitis B, no cirrhosis — ultrasound + AFP every 6 months
  2. Brother with nasopharyngeal carcinoma — EBV DNA and/or nasopharyngoscopy
  3. Average-risk 50/F — CA-125 + transvaginal ultrasound for ovarian cancer
  4. 60/M, 30 pack-years — annual low-dose CT

C. CA-125 + TVUS did not reduce mortality in average-risk women and can lead to major surgery from false positives.

A screening study reports that 5-year survival after diagnosis rose from 40% to 65% in the screened group, but the age-adjusted death rate from that cancer did not change. The best explanation is:

  1. Screening is effective; survival is the right endpoint
  2. Lead-time bias: diagnosis came earlier but death did not come later
  3. Selection of sicker patients into the screening arm
  4. False-negative results lowering survival

B. Judge screening by mortality, not survival after diagnosis. The survival clock simply started earlier.

An 84/M in a nursing home has a small low-grade prostate cancer found on routine PSA. He dies 2 years later of heart failure with no prostate symptoms. This case best illustrates:

  1. Lead-time bias
  2. Length bias
  3. False-positive result
  4. Overdiagnosis

D. A real cancer that would never have caused harm. Length bias is about slow vs fast tumors being found, not about cancers that never matter.

A side effect shared by tamoxifen and raloxifene used for breast cancer chemoprevention is:

  1. Venous thromboembolism
  2. Endometrial cancer
  3. Osteoporosis
  4. Bleeding

A. Raloxifene spares the uterus but not the veins. Endometrial cancer is tamoxifen's; osteoporosis is the aromatase inhibitors'; bleeding is aspirin's.

Match the intervention with the step of carcinogenesis it mainly interrupts, per the lecture. Which pairing is correct?

  1. Screening — initiation
  2. Smoking cessation — progression
  3. HPV vaccination — promotion
  4. Sun avoidance — progression

C. Lecture: initiation ← exercise, quitting smoking, sun avoidance; promotion ← vaccination; progression ← screening.

A 9-year-old Burkitt lymphoma patient starts induction chemotherapy. Two days later: K 6.4, phosphate high, calcium low, uric acid 14, creatinine rising. Which measure should have been the priority beforehand? Harrison's

  1. Urine alkalinization with bicarbonate
  2. Allopurinol with aggressive IV hydration before chemotherapy
  3. High-dose dexamethasone
  4. Calcium gluconate infusion before each cycle

B. Tumor lysis syndrome: prevention (allopurinol + fluids) is the key step. Urine alkalinization is no longer advised.

Last-look cram sheet

  • Frame: Diagnosis (tissue) → Stage → Plan → Support. No tissue → biopsy. Tissue in hand → stage.
  • Old keys: "priority once cancer is established" = disclosure of diagnosis (2027 and 2028).
  • FNAB → thyroid. CUP → history + focused search + biopsy nearest accessible tissue. NGS = predictive.
  • TNM most common · Ann Arbor = Hodgkin · Dukes = CRC (TNM still used) · FIGO = gyne. T by size (breast) / depth (CRC, uterus).
  • Clinical stage = before the knife; pathologic = after the knife.
  • ECOG 0 active · 1 light work · 2 up, self-care, no work · 3 bed/chair >50% · 4 disabled · 5 dead. KPS 100/70/50/0.
  • ECOG 3–4 = limited options, unless reversible (hypercalcemia, dehydration, pain). PS is a finding, not a verdict.
  • Markers monitor, rarely diagnose. CEA ↑ in IBD/smoking; CA-125 ↑ in menses/pregnancy; AFP ↑ in cirrhosis; PSA ↑ in BPH.
  • Curative = early, accepts toxicity, combined modalities. Palliative = advanced, low toxicity tolerance.
  • RECIST partial ≥30% · WHO partial >50% · progression 20% ↑ or any new lesion.
  • Pain 70% tumor. Nausea: acute <24 h, delayed 1–7 d, anticipatory = before. Depression ~25%.
  • Nutrition: >10% weight loss, albumin <3.4, transferrin <150 → enteral first.
  • Effusion: tap → chest tube (recurs <2 wk) → pleurodesis. Tamponade → window. Lung/breast/lymphoma = 75%.
  • Infection = #1 cause of death in cancer patients; heart disease #1 overall, cancer #2. Age = #1 risk factor.
  • Primary = no cancer · Secondary = screening · Tertiary = treatment. Tobacco first (quitting → 30–50% lower 10-y lung-ca mortality).
  • Initiation ← lifestyle · Promotion ← vaccine · Progression ← screening.
  • Asbestos → mesothelioma; aromatic amines → bladder; alcohol → breast/liver/esophagus/H&N; UV → mostly SCC.
  • Beta carotene → more lung cancer in smokers. Aspirin → fewer CRC, bleeding. Tamoxifen → endometrial ca + VTE; raloxifene → VTE. Finasteride not FDA-approved.
  • HBV → HCC · HPV 16/18 → cervix + oropharynx · H. pylori → gastric. FAP → colectomy · BRCA → mastectomy/salpingo-oophorectomy.
  • Lead-time = clock starts earlier · Length = slow tumors found · Overdiagnosis = never would matter. Judge by mortality.
  • PHEX: cervix 30–65 cytology q3y / HPV q5y · breast 50–69 mammo q1–2y (yearly if FHx/BRCA) · CRC 50 FIT yearly → colonoscopy · lung 50–80 >20 PY LDCT yearly · HCC US + AFP q6mo · NPC relative → EBV DNA · prostate = blue shared decision.
  • CXR screening: no benefit. MCED, whole-body CT, tumor-marker panels: not for screening.

2.06 Introduction to Radiology I 5 items

Dr. Christine Carlos-Depaynos · Recall 3 / Comp 2 / App 0 / Analysis 0 · Past-exam style source: 2028 #95–100 and 2027 #96–100 (same professor, so trust both)

How Dr. Carlos-Depaynos asks
  • One-line recall stems: "How does X appear on Y?", "Which modality…?", "What do you call…?" No cases.
  • Her favorites: density words (radiolucent vs radiopaque vs hyperdense), radiation (which one is high dose, which have none), best modality for (soft tissue, fracture, meniscus), fluoroscopy, marker / teleroentgenogram.
  • Distractors are always the same idea in another modality's word (hyperdense vs radiopaque vs hyperintense vs hyperechoic). Match the word to the modality first.
  • Teleroentgenogram came up both years, even though it isn't in the 2026 2.06 trans. Learn the 4 criteria.
Past-exam concept map (2027 / 2028)
Concept20282027Covered in
Air / calcium appearance on X-ray (radiolucent / radiopaque)#95#98Densities
White on MRI = hyperintense (terms per modality)#98—Black/white terms
High-dose ionizing = CT—#97Modality summary
Superior soft tissue = MRI; fracture = CT; meniscus = MRI#99, #100#96Best modality
Fluoroscopy = continuous beam, real time#96—X-ray types
Marker on patient's right—#99Orientation
Teleroentgenogram (PA view, criteria)#97#100Orientation

The 5 X-ray densities HIGH-YIELD 2028 #95 2027 #98

Whitest → blackest: bone/calcium → soft tissue → water → fat → air. Metal is whiter than all of them.

Rank (white → black)DensityOn X-ray
0 (brightest)Metal (coin, orthopedic device)Bright white, most opaque
1Bone / calciumWhite, most radiopaque of the 5
2Soft tissueLight gray
3Water / fluidGray
4FatDark gray
5 (darkest)Air (lungs, trachea, bowel gas)Black, most radiolucent (lets the most X-rays through)
  • Dense tissue absorbs X-rays and looks white. Thin tissue lets X-rays pass through to the film and looks black.
  • Mnemonic, black → white: Andrew Felt Sorry For Cursing Mammography = Air, Fat, Soft tissue/Fluid, Calcium, Metal. p. 4
  • "Density" means how black or white something looks. The word is used especially for CT. p. 4
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "How does [air / calcium / bone] appear on a conventional radiograph?"
  • Trap: hyperdense or hypodense are offered as choices. Those are CT words. On a plain X-ray the answer is always radiolucent (black) or radiopaque (white). Also watch the direction: the mnemonic runs black → white, but the trans figure runs white → black.

On a plain abdominal radiograph, which structure is expected to be more radiolucent than fat?

  1. Urine in the bladder
  2. Gas in the colon
  3. Liver
  4. Calcified gallstone

B. Only air is blacker than fat. Urine (water) and liver (soft tissue) are whiter than fat, and calcium is radiopaque.

Black vs white: each modality has its own word MUST KNOW 2028 #98

Hypo = black, hyper = white. X-ray is the exception: radiolucent = black, radiopaque = white.

ModalityBlack (dark)White (bright)Root word
X-rayRadiolucent ("lucency")Radiopaque ("opacity")lucent / opaque
CTHypodenseHyperdensedensity
UltrasoundHypoechoicHyperechoic (echogenic)echo
MRIHypointenseHyperintensesignal intensity
  • Link the word to the physics: CT measures density, ultrasound records echoes, MRI reads signal intensity. p. 3
  • "Echogenic" means the same as hyperechoic. It is a common ultrasound word but isn't in the trans table.
  • "Isodense" (same as the surrounding tissue) is a distractor. It is not in the trans.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "What do you call a structure that is white / dark on [modality]?" or "Which pairing is INCORRECT?"
  • Trap: all 4 choices mean the same color. Pick the one whose root word matches the modality in the stem.

A renal cyst looks dark on ultrasound. In the sonologist's report, the cyst is described as:

  1. Hypoechoic
  2. Hypodense
  3. Radiolucent
  4. Hypointense

A. Dark on ultrasound is hypoechoic. Hypodense is the CT word, radiolucent is the X-ray word, and hypointense is the MRI word.

Not in the 2026 trans: MRI T1 vs T2, CT Hounsfield units (skim only)

The trans says MRI physics won't be tested (p. 3). This is only here in case a distractor uses these words. Standard radiology, not trans

T1T2
FatBright (hyperintense)Bright / intermediate
Water / fluid (CSF, edema)Dark (hypointense)Bright ("T2 = water white")
Cortical bone, airDarkDark

CT Hounsfield units: air about −1000, fat about −100, water 0, soft tissue +20 to +80, bone +400 to +1000 or more. The order is the same as the 5 densities.

Gadolinium (the MRI contrast agent) makes protons realign faster, so the tissue looks brighter. This part is in the trans. p. 3

Modality summary: radiation, strengths, weaknesses LECTURER 2027 #97

Ionizing: X-ray (low dose) and CT (high dose). No ionizing radiation: MRI and ultrasound (the lecturer emphasized this).

ModalityRadiation?Best forPoor for / problemContrast
X-rayYes, low doseBones, metal (orthopedic devices), calcium. Cheap and available.Cartilage and soft tissue, intra-abdominal organs. 2D only.None (angiography uses iodinated)
CTYes, high doseGood soft tissue, detailed bone, calcification (better than X-ray)Cartilage and ligaments. Metal causes streak artifact. Quite expensive.Iodinated
MRINone (magnetic fields + radio waves + field gradients)Superior soft tissue: ligaments, bone marrow, spinal cord. Images in any plane.Motion artifact (slow scan). Unsafe with non-MRI-compatible metal or electronic devices and shrapnel. Claustrophobia. Most expensive, not in all hospitals.Gadolinium
UltrasoundNone (high-frequency sound, pulse-echo)Solid organs, fluid-filled organs, superficial small parts, real time, vessels (Doppler)Air (lungs), bone and anything behind bone. Operator dependent.None
TRAP Fluoroscopy is an X-ray, but its continuous beam increases radiation exposure, so don't call it low dose. Metal is a strength on X-ray, causes streak artifact on CT, and is a safety problem on MRI. p. 2–3

A 24-year-old pregnant woman needs abdominal imaging. Which pair of modalities avoids ionizing radiation completely?

  1. CT scan and fluoroscopy
  2. X-ray and ultrasound
  3. CT scan and MRI
  4. Ultrasound and MRI

D. Only ultrasound (sound waves) and MRI (magnets and radio waves) are non-ionizing. Each of the other pairs includes an X-ray–based modality.

Pick the modality HIGH-YIELD 2027 #96 2028 #99 2028 #100

Soft tissue gets better as you go X-ray (poor) → CT (good) → MRI (superior). Fine bone detail and calcification → CT.

Stem says…Answer
Superior soft tissue contrast. Ligament, meniscus/cartilage, spinal cord, bone marrow.MRI
Fracture or detailed bone evaluation (when plain X-ray isn't a choice). Calcified lesion in a patient with a non-MRI-compatible device.CT
Bones, metal implants, calcium. Cheap first look.X-ray
Solid or fluid organ, superficial part, vessels by Doppler, real timeUltrasound
Moving structures: peristalsis, diaphragm, heart, barium, catheter placementFluoroscopy
Contrast flowing through vessels in real timeConventional angiography
Operating room, patient can't be moved (ORIF, intraoperative cholangiogram)C-arm X-ray
TRAP In 2028 #99 the key for "best for bone fractures" was CT, because plain X-ray wasn't among the choices (CT = "detailed bone evaluation", p. 3). If both X-ray and CT are offered, read the stem: "cheap, initial" points to X-ray; "detailed or complex" points to CT. A meniscus is cartilage, and cartilage is a CT weakness, so the answer is MRI.

A 19-year-old basketball player twisted his knee and now has instability. An anterior cruciate ligament tear is suspected. Which imaging best shows it?

  1. Plain radiograph
  2. CT scan
  3. MRI
  4. Fluoroscopy

C. Ligaments need MRI's superior soft tissue contrast. On CT, cartilage and ligaments are listed as weaknesses, and X-ray soft tissue contrast is poor.

Fluoroscopy and the other X-ray types 2028 #96

Fluoroscopy = "real-time X-ray": a continuous beam passes through the patient onto a fluorescing screen or monitor.

TypeKey feature
FluoroscopyContinuous beam, moving structures (GI peristalsis, diaphragm, cardiac action, barium, catheters). More radiation.
Conventional angiographyFluoroscopy plus iodinated contrast injected into vessels. Used to study blood vessels.
CR vs DRCR uses a phosphor plate that is read manually (slower). DR uses a fixed electronic detector/CCD, is cassette-less, and gives an immediate image.
C-armX-ray machine brought into the OR
CT typesConventional = one slice at a time (15–30 min for a cranial study). Helical = continuous. MDCT = multiple detector rows, one breath hold.

A patient with suspected left phrenic nerve palsy is asked to sniff while the radiologist watches the hemidiaphragms move on a monitor. This study is:

  1. Conventional angiography
  2. Fluoroscopy
  3. Digital radiography
  4. Helical CT

B. Watching motion in real time with a continuous beam is fluoroscopy. Angiography would need contrast injected into vessels.

Marker, orientation and teleroentgenogram HIGH-YIELD 2027 #99 2027 #100 2028 #97

The marker always goes on the patient's right, and you view the film as if facing the patient (patient's right = viewer's left). A teleroentgenogram is taken in the PA view.

  • Position = the patient's posture (upright, supine, prone, lateral decubitus). Projection = the beam direction from source to surface (AP, PA, lateral). p. 4
  • Axial CT follows the same rule: patient's right on the viewer's left, anterior at the top. p. 5
  • Swallowed coin: an AP film can't tell trachea from esophagus. On the lateral view, a coin behind the tracheal air lucency is in the upper esophagus. p. 4
TELEROENTGENOGRAM criteria (not in the 2026 2.06 trans. Source: 2028 #97 rationale and the 2027 Radiology III trans.)
PA projection · patient upright · arms akimbo (hands on waist or behind head, so the scapulae move off the lung fields) · taken at mid or full inspiration.
The usual 6-ft (72 in) tube-to-film distance reduces heart magnification. Standard radiology, not trans
TRAP "Supine", "AP" and "hands at the sides" are all wrong for a teleroentgenogram. In 2028 #97 the key was "PA view" over "chest in full expansion", so when only one choice is accepted, PA is the defining criterion.

Which radiographic technique is NOT appropriate when taking a teleroentgenogram?

  1. Patient supine with the beam entering anteriorly
  2. Patient upright
  3. Arms akimbo
  4. Film taken at full inspiration

A. A supine film with the beam entering from the front is an AP film. A teleroentgenogram is an upright PA film.

Practice drill — Dr. Carlos-Depaynos style

On a plain radiograph, which order goes correctly from most radiolucent to most radiopaque?

  1. Fat → air → water → soft tissue → bone
  2. Air → water → fat → soft tissue → bone
  3. Air → fat → water → soft tissue → bone
  4. Bone → soft tissue → water → fat → air

C. Black → white is air, fat, water, soft tissue, bone. D is the correct order but in the opposite direction from what was asked.

Which modality–term pair for a bright/white structure is INCORRECT?

  1. CT – hyperdense
  2. Ultrasound – hyperechoic
  3. MRI – hyperintense
  4. Plain radiograph – radiolucent

D. Radiolucent means black. White on X-ray is radiopaque.

A 68-year-old man with a hip prosthesis is followed up to check where the metal hardware sits. Which modality images the metal well at the lowest cost?

  1. CT scan
  2. Plain radiograph
  3. MRI
  4. Ultrasound

B. X-ray is good for metals (orthopedic devices) and is cheap. On CT, metal causes streak artifact. On MRI, metal is a safety problem.

Which of the following is a limitation of ultrasound?

  1. Poor visualization of air-filled lungs
  2. High dose of ionizing radiation
  3. Unsafe with metallic shrapnel
  4. Cannot image in real time

A. Ultrasound can't see through air or bone. It is non-ionizing and real time. The shrapnel problem belongs to MRI.

A patient with a non-MRI-compatible cardiac pacemaker has a suspected calcified intracranial lesion. Best modality?

  1. MRI with gadolinium
  2. Ultrasound
  3. CT scan
  4. Fluoroscopy

C. CT evaluates calcification better than X-ray, and MRI is unsafe with the device. Ultrasound can't see through the skull.

Which statement about MRI is TRUE?

  1. It uses low-dose ionizing radiation
  2. Its contrast agent is iodinated
  3. Its main artifact is the streak artifact from metal
  4. It gives superior soft tissue contrast, such as for the spinal cord

D. MRI is non-ionizing, its contrast is gadolinium, and its typical artifact is motion. Streak artifact from metal is a CT problem.

Which X-ray–based study exposes the patient to more radiation because of its continuous beam?

  1. Computed radiography
  2. Fluoroscopy
  3. Digital radiography
  4. Film radiography

B. Fluoroscopy uses a continuous beam to show real-time motion, which increases exposure. The others are single exposures.

Last-look cram sheet

  • Whitest → blackest: bone → soft tissue → water → fat → air. Metal is the brightest of all. Air = most radiolucent.
  • Black/white words: X-ray radiolucent/radiopaque · CT hypo/hyperdense · US hypo/hyperechoic · MRI hypo/hyperintense.
  • Ionizing: X-ray (low dose), CT (high dose), fluoroscopy (more exposure). Non-ionizing: MRI, US.
  • Superior soft tissue, ligament, meniscus, spinal cord, marrow → MRI.
  • Detailed bone, fracture (no X-ray choice), calcification → CT. Metal on CT → streak artifact.
  • Metal implants, bones, cheap → X-ray (2D only, poor soft tissue).
  • US: solid, fluid and superficial organs, Doppler, real time. Poor for air and bone. Operator dependent.
  • Continuous beam, real-time motion → fluoroscopy. Plus iodinated contrast in vessels → angiography.
  • Contrast: CT and angiography = iodinated. MRI = gadolinium (makes tissue brighter).
  • Marker on the patient's right (appears on the viewer's left).
  • Teleroentgenogram: PA, upright, arms akimbo, inspiration.
  • Coin behind the tracheal air on the lateral view → upper esophagus.

LE1 Rapid Recall 10 items

2 items each: Communication (Dr. Castillo) · History Taking (Dr. Rosario) · PE / General Survey / Vitals (Dr. Lista) · Ophthalmology (Dr. Aclan) · ENT (Dr. Miura) · Past-exam style source: 2027 LE2 #101–110, 2028 LE2 #101–110, 2029 LE1

How LE1 recall shows up in LE2
  • 2 short items per LE1 lecture, placed at the very end (#101–110). Mostly recall or one-step application.
  • Communication and history questions give a quoted doctor line and ask you to name the technique (summarization, topic tracking, empathic response).
  • PE questions ask about positions and technique (standing for the spine, supine with knees bent for the abdomen), BMI, or precautions.
  • Ophtha questions give a finding and ask for the test or diagnosis (confrontation test, oscillopsia, episcleritis, macular degeneration).
  • ENT questions ask for a tuning-fork interpretation, a "NOT" structure or maneuver, or a duct.

Concept202820272029 LE1

Wharton's duct; posterior rhinoscopy structures—#109, #110#67

Physician–Patient Communication HIGH-YIELD 2028 #101–102 2027 #101

Patient-centered (biopsychosocial) communication is the gold standard. Physician-centered (biomedical) communication is fastest in acute cases. Best practice: let the patient talk first, then shift to clinician-led questions.

Biomedical (physician-centered)Biopsychosocial (patient-centered)
Who directsClinician takes charge to identify a disease. 70% of MDs use it.Patient tells what matters most to them. This is the gold standard.
PlusEfficient for quick diagnosis, acute casesGives the personal context, feelings and concerns
MinusDepersonalizing; misses psychosocial factors; ↓ satisfaction and shared decision-makingTakes more time
TechniqueHow to recognize it
Continuers (facilitation)"Mm-hmm… go on… I'm listening"
EchoingRepeats the patient's word: "Spread?" "Going to die?"
Graded response"How many steps can you climb before you get short of breath?"
Multiple-choice answers"Aching, sharp, burning…?" This is acceptable 2027 #101
ValidationTreats the emotion as legitimate ("anyone would feel that way"), which builds connection
ReassuranceComes only after the feelings are acknowledged. Be careful not to give false hope.
PartneringCommits to an ongoing relationship ("we'll work on your asthma together")
Transitions"Next I'll ask about…". Tells the patient the interview is changing direction (e.g., before STD questions).
SummarizationA capsule summary that shows you were listening carefully 2028 #101
EmpoweringDraws out the patient's view, makes your reasoning transparent, admits the limits of what you know
  • 7 goals: fostering the relationship, gathering information, providing information, decision-making, enabling treatment-related behavior, responding to emotions, managing uncertainty. LE1 asked you to match quotes to goals.
  • 3 components: verbal is only 10% of the message. Nonverbal plus paraverbal (tone, pitch, pace) make up 90%.
  • Most important barrier: lack of insight (poor communication training).
  • Rapport breaks the initial barrier. It builds trust, so the patient is willing to share sensitive information 2028 #102.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: a quoted doctor line → name the technique or goal.
  • Trap: validation vs reassurance. How to tell: validation says "your feeling makes sense", while reassurance says "it will be OK". Summarization vs echoing: summarization restates the whole story, echoing repeats a single word.

History Taking, Symptom Analysis, Temporal Profile HIGH-YIELD 2028 #103 2027 #102–104

Start with rapport, then use open-ended questions before focused ones. Characterize each symptom with PQRSTU. Write the chief complaint as a symptom plus its duration, never a diagnosis. Draw the temporal profile after the ROS and before the PE.

ItemKey points
Interview sequence1 Greet and build rapport (first) → 2 Invite the story → 3 Set the agenda → 4 Expand the story and test hypotheses → 5 Shared understanding → 6 Negotiate a plan → 7 Follow-up and closing
Mindful practiceObserving your own thought process, e.g., pausing before lecturing a non-compliant patient
Topic trackingKeeping to a mutually agreed topic through summarizing, process transparency and goal alignment ("stay with diabetes or shift to back pain?") 2027 #103
Empathic clue acknowledgement"It sounds like you're afraid… tell me more." Empathic responses: "How did you feel about that?" 2027 #102
Question typesLoaded = biased, with unjustified assumptions. Leading = "Isn't it true that…". Simple direct = yes/no. Neutral = "Tell me more…". Focusing = steers back to a topic the patient already raised.
PQRSTUProvocative/Palliative · Quality/Quantity · Region/Radiation · Severity (x/10) · Timing · Understanding ("What do you think is causing it?")
FormatPatient profile → Source and reliability (poor/fair/good or %) → CC → HPI → Past health → Family hx → ROS → Temporal profile
Chief complaintBrief. One or two symptoms at most, in the patient's own words, with duration, and no diagnostic labels ("Chest heaviness, 2 hours" is correct; "Unstable angina, r/o MI" is wrong)
Sensitive historyRelatives present → ask the patient if he's comfortable answering with them there. If not, politely ask them to step out 2027 #104. CAGE screens for alcohol use. Pack-years = packs/day × years.
Temporal patternClue
IntermittentAlternately occurs and ceases completely (can happen several times a day)
ContinuousNo break
RemittentFluctuates but never returns to baseline
RecurrentThe whole episode repeats at intervals of hours or days
PeriodicClusters lasting days, weeks or months; the symptom-free period is longer than the symptomatic period
  • Temporal profile: use 1–2 symptom lines (max 3) and a separate diagram for each illness. The order of symptoms changes the diagnosis: fever → abdominal pain → jaundice suggests viral hepatitis, while abdominal pain → jaundice → fever suggests gallstone with cholecystitis.
  • 4 phases of the HPI: (1) open-ended neutral account → (2) detailed analysis with closed-neutral questions → (3) test the possibilities with other symptoms → (4) ROS.
  • Pertinent negatives narrow the differential. Subjective data (history) and objective data (PE, labs) complement each other.
Note: the 1.02 trans uses PQRSTU (1.01 and ENT use CLITAAA: Character, Location, Intensity, Timing, Associated, Aggravating/Alleviating). "OLDCARTS" is not in the trans.

Complete PE, General Survey, Vital Signs HIGH-YIELD 2028 #105–106 2027 #105–106

Examine from the patient's right. Use the same head-to-toe order every time. Change the patient's position only when needed. Use IPPA everywhere except the abdomen, which is IAPP.

Vital signTechnique / cutoff
BPCuff at heart level. Palpate the systolic first, then inflate 30 mmHg above it. Use the bell (Korotkoff sounds are low-pitched). Deflate at 2–3 mmHg/s. Systolic = first of ≥2 consecutive sounds; diastolic = disappearance.
OrthostaticMeasure supine after 3–10 min rest, then within 3 min of standing. Positive if SBP falls ≥20 or DBP falls ≥10 mmHg.
Heart rateRadial pulse. If regular, count 30 s × 2; if too fast, too slow or irregular, count a full 60 s. Normal range is 60 to 90–100/min.
Resp. rateCount quietly, by inspection or over the trachea, while still "taking the pulse". Patients change their breathing once they notice.
TemperatureOral, rectal, axillary, tympanic or temporal
BMI (kg/m²)WHOAsia-Pacific (lecturer: "more applicable")
<18.5UnderweightUnderweight
18.5–22.9Healthy (to 24.9)Normal
23–24.9HealthyOverweight, at risk
25–29.9OverweightObese I
30–34.9 / 35–39.9 / ≥40Obese I / II / IIIObese II (≥30)
  • General survey begins the moment you meet the patient: apparent health, LOC, signs of distress, skin color, dress/grooming/hygiene, facial expression, odors, posture/gait/motor activity, height/weight/BMI. If BMI If BMI ≥35, measure the waist. Risk rises at ≥35 in (women) and ≥45 in (men).gt;35, measure the waist. Risk rises at If BMI ≥35, measure the waist. Risk rises at ≥35 in (women) and ≥45 in (men).gt;35 in (women) and If BMI ≥35, measure the waist. Risk rises at ≥35 in (women) and ≥45 in (men).gt;45 in (men) per 1.03 trans. Bates uses If BMI ≥35, measure the waist. Risk rises at ≥35 in (women) and ≥45 in (men).gt;40 in for men, so answer with the trans number.
  • Right side: JVP estimates are more reliable, the hand rests on the apical impulse, and the right kidney is more often palpable. Tangential light shows the JVP, thyroid and apical impulse.
  • Positions: CV exam at 30° (left lateral decubitus for S3/MS; sit, lean forward and exhale for AR). Abdomen: supine with knees bent to relax the abdominal muscles 2028 #105. Standing: varicose veins, spine alignment 2027 #105, hernias, gait, Romberg.
  • Forgot a step? Go back to it calmly, even out of sequence. Drape so only the area being examined is exposed (re-drape the R breast, then expose the L).
  • Precautions: standard precautions cover all fluids except sweat. Universal precautions cover bloodborne pathogens (blood, semen, vaginal secretions, CSF, pleural fluid, etc.). Use soap and water if hands are visibly soiled or after C. difficile/norovirus; otherwise alcohol rub. Contact precautions = gloves + gown (protect staff and others) 2028 #106. Droplet (influenza, meningococcus, pertussis) = surgical mask. Airborne (TB, measles, varicella) = N95 + negative-pressure room. Needlestick → wash and report immediately.
TRAP BMI has been asked before using WHO cutoffs (2027 #106, LE1 #52). If the stem says "Asian" or "more applicable", use Asia-Pacific: a BMI of 25.5 is "overweight" by WHO but "obese I" by Asia-Pacific.

Ophthalmic History and PE from LE1 exam rationales — ophtha trans unavailable 2027 #107–108 2028 #107–108

Visual acuity is the "vital sign of the eye" and is done first, before the eye is manipulated (especially in trauma or open globe). For other questions, match the finding to the test.

TestChecks
Confrontation testVisual fields, i.e., lesions of the visual pathway (pituitary adenoma with temporal field loss). Asked twice.
Corneal light reflex (Hirschberg)Ocular alignment
RetinoscopyRefractive error (objective)
Swinging flashlightRAPD / Marcus Gunn pupil: the affected pupil dilates when light swings to it, pointing to the optic nerve (optic neuritis)
TonometryGoldmann applanation = gold standard. iCare/rebound and air-puff are screening tools. No digital tonometry in an open globe.
Direct ophthalmoscopy (dark room)Media/red reflex, optic disc (cup-disc ratio, color, borders), vessels, retinal background (hemorrhages, exudates), macula. Not the limbus or retinal thickness.
  • VA ladder: Snellen at 20 ft (6 m). If the patient can't read it, they walk closer. If they can't read it at 1 m → count fingers → hand movement → light projection → light perception. Near card (Jaeger) is held at 14 in (35 cm). Use the tumbling E for illiterate patients.
  • Light projection: 4/4 quadrants = good · 2–3/4 = fair · 1/4 = poor · 0/4 = negative.
  • Red reflex: absent or dull with media opacity (cataract, corneal scar). It stays bright in myopia, dry eye and mild diabetic retinopathy.
  • Near response = pupillary constriction + convergence (medial recti) + accommodation (ciliary muscle contracts, lens becomes more convex).
  • Discharge: allergic = clear and stringy with itch · bacterial = mucopurulent with crusting · viral = watery with redness.
  • Red eye with pain = scleritis (deep, boring, worse with eye movement). Episcleritis = localized and usually painless 2028 #107. Subconjunctival hemorrhage = painless. Hordeolum = painful, tender, red lid-margin lump; chalazion = painless.
  • Nystagmus → oscillopsia 2027 #108. Difficulty recognizing faces with peripheral vision intact → macular degeneration 2028 #108. Distant blur in a young adult → myopia; age-related near blur → presbyopia.
  • Previous eye surgery or trauma and spectacle use belong in the past ocular history, not the past medical history.

PE of ENT HIGH-YIELD 2028 #109–110 2027 #109–110

In conductive loss, Weber lateralizes to the bad ear and Rinne is negative (BC > AC). In sensorineural loss, Weber lateralizes to the good ear and Rinne stays positive (AC > BC).

Weber (midline: vertex, glabella, nasal bridge, mentum, not the mastoid)Rinne (mastoid → beside the ear canal, tines parallel to it)
NormalHeard equallyAC > BC (positive)
ConductiveLouder in the affected earBC > AC (negative); if negative or equal, do threshold testing
SensorineuralLouder in the normal earAC > BC, with a shorter duration
  • Setup: patient sits upright (never straddle). 100-W unfrosted bulb behind the patient. Head mirror over the dominant eye (focal length 14 in). 512 Hz fork is best; strike it near the base on your hand.
  • Ear: examine the healthy ear first. Pull the pinna up, back and out in adults (back and down in children). Use the largest speculum that fits so it can't slide into the painful bony canal. The cone of light is anteroinferior and is only a reflection. TM mobility: pneumatic/Siegel otoscope, Valsalva (pinch nose and blow), Toynbee (pinch nose and swallow). Epley is not one; it treats BPPV 2028 #110. Finger rub is positive if >2 of 6 attempts are missed.
  • Anterior rhinoscopy: hold the speculum in the non-dominant hand. Open the blades laterally, away from the septum, and withdraw them partly open. Kiesselbach's plexus is on the anterior septum. Pale, boggy turbinates with watery discharge = allergic; purulent discharge = bacterial. A mass or polyp → endoscopy.
  • Posterior rhinoscopy: depress the anterior ⅔ of the tongue and use a small nasopharyngeal mirror facing up. Patient breathes through the nose so the soft palate drops. You see the choanae, septum, middle turbinate, eustachian tube opening, tubal tonsil and Rosenmüller fossa. Not Kiesselbach's 2027 #110.
  • Indirect laryngoscopy: sniffing position. Patient breathes through the mouth. Hold the tongue with gauze; the laryngeal mirror faces down and is warmed to prevent fogging. Avoid the posterior ⅓ of the tongue (gag); the uvula is OK. Use xylocaine if the patient gags a lot. High-pitched "eee" = vocal folds adduct; "hee-hee" = they abduct. An immobile fold = paralysis.
  • Mouth/neck: Stensen's duct (parotid) opens opposite the upper 2nd molar. Wharton's duct (submandibular) opens in the floor of the mouth 2027 #109. The thyroid rises on swallowing and is examined from behind. Lymph drainage: lips → IA; anterior ⅔ of tongue and floor of mouth → IB; nasopharynx → II.
TRAP "Weber lateralizes to the right" is ambiguous on its own: it can mean right conductive OR left sensorineural loss. The Rinne result decides. If Rinne is negative (BC > AC) on the side Weber points to, the loss is conductive on that side.

Practice drill — LE1 recall (2 per lecture)

A 50/F caring alone for her bedridden mother cries during the interview. The physician says: "Anyone looking after a sick parent by herself would feel exhausted. What you're feeling makes complete sense." Which skilled-interviewing technique is this?

  1. Validation
  2. Reassurance
  3. Partnering
  4. Summarization

A. Validation affirms that the emotion is legitimate. Reassurance ("everything will be all right") promises a good outcome, and the trans warns it can give false hope.

A 62/M is brought to the ER pale, diaphoretic and clutching his chest. Which communication approach is most appropriate for the initial interview, and why?

  1. Biopsychosocial, because it is the gold standard and must always come first
  2. Biopsychosocial, because it gives the quickest diagnosis
  3. Biomedical, because it is efficient for quick diagnosis in acute situations
  4. Biomedical, because it raises patient satisfaction and shared decision-making

C. The physician-centered style is efficient in acute settings. Its known weakness is lower satisfaction and less shared decision-making (D is reversed).

A 24/M has had fever for 6 days. His temperature swings between 37.9 and 39.6 °C each day but never returns to normal between the peaks. Which temporal profile pattern does this show?

  1. Intermittent
  2. Periodic
  3. Recurrent
  4. Remittent

D. Remittent means the symptom fluctuates but never returns to baseline. In an intermittent pattern the symptom ceases completely between episodes.

On admission, a 58/F tells the clerk she "has a heart problem and high blood" and has felt dizzy for 3 days, with nausea since yesterday. Which chief complaint is written correctly?

  1. "Hypertensive urgency, rule out stroke"
  2. "Dizziness, 3 days"
  3. "Heart problem and high blood"
  4. "Dizziness, nausea, vomiting, headache, and weakness"

B. A chief complaint is a concrete symptom (two at most) with its duration, in the patient's words. A and C are diagnostic labels. D lists too many symptoms and has no duration.

A 45/M Filipino office worker weighs 72 kg and is 168 cm tall. Using the BMI classification the lecturer called more applicable in clinical practice, how is he classified?

  1. Overweight
  2. Overweight, at risk
  3. Obese I
  4. Obese II

C. 72 ÷ 1.68² = 25.5 kg/m². Asia-Pacific obese I is 25–29.9. "Overweight" (A) is the WHO class, the trap.

A 72/M on antihypertensives reports lightheadedness on getting up. After 5 minutes supine his BP is 130/84; 2 minutes after standing it is 116/72. What is the correct interpretation?

  1. Orthostatic hypotension, because diastolic pressure fell by at least 10 mmHg within 3 minutes
  2. Normal, because systolic pressure fell by less than 20 mmHg
  3. Not interpretable, because he must stand for at least 10 minutes
  4. Not interpretable, because he must rest supine for at least 15 minutes first

A. SBP fell 14 (less than 20) but DBP fell 12 (at least 10). Either criterion within 3 minutes of standing is enough. B looks only at the systolic drop.

A 26/F has had blurred vision and pain on moving her right eye for 4 days. When the light is swung from her left eye to her right eye, both pupils dilate. What does this finding mean?

  1. A normal near response
  2. A left relative afferent pupillary defect from cataract
  3. Right ocular misalignment detected by the Hirschberg test
  4. A right relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil), suggesting an optic nerve problem

D. In the swinging flashlight test, paradoxical dilation when light reaches the affected eye is an RAPD of that eye (here optic neuritis OD). Hirschberg tests alignment, not pupils.

Which finding–diagnosis pair is INCORRECT?

  1. Clear, stringy discharge with intense itching: allergic conjunctivitis
  2. Mucopurulent discharge with lid crusting: bacterial conjunctivitis
  3. Painless, non-tender nodule at the lid margin: hordeolum
  4. Images that seem to bounce when fixating: nystagmus

C. A hordeolum is a painful, tender, red lid-margin mass (acute infection). A painless lid nodule is a chalazion.

A 35/F says her hearing is muffled in the left ear. Weber lateralizes to the LEFT. Rinne shows BC > AC on the left and AC > BC on the right. What is the most likely cause?

  1. Right sensorineural loss from noise exposure
  2. Cerumen impaction in the left ear
  3. Left sensorineural hearing loss
  4. Right otitis media

B. Weber toward the affected ear plus a negative Rinne on that side means left conductive loss (cerumen, otitis media, TM or ossicle disease). Right SNHL (A) would also send Weber left, but the left Rinne would stay positive.

During indirect laryngoscopy, the examiner wants to see the vocal folds open (abduct) to check their movement. What should the patient be asked to do?

  1. Breathe through the nose
  2. Swallow repeatedly
  3. Say a high-pitched "eee"
  4. Say "hee-hee"

D. "Hee-hee" makes the folds abduct during the pause to breathe. A high-pitched "eee" makes them adduct. Nose breathing is the instruction for posterior rhinoscopy, not laryngoscopy.

Last-look cram sheet

  • Gold standard = patient-centered. Biomedical is fast in acute cases but misses psychosocial factors. Verbal is only 10% of communication.
  • Capsule summary → summarization. "Spread?" → echoing. "Stay with diabetes or shift to back pain?" → topic tracking / goal alignment. Pausing to check your own assumptions → mindful practice.
  • Interview step 1 = greet and build rapport. CC = symptom + duration, no diagnosis. Temporal profile comes after ROS, before PE.
  • Periodic = symptom-free period longer than the clusters. Remittent = never back to baseline. Intermittent = ceases completely.
  • BP: palpate, then inflate +30 mmHg, bell, deflate 2–3 mmHg/s. Orthostatic = SBP drop ≥20 or DBP drop ≥10 within 3 min of standing.
  • Examine from the right. Abdomen = IAPP, supine with knees bent. Spine alignment and varicose veins are checked standing.
  • Asia-Pacific BMI: ≥23 overweight, 25 obese I, 30 obese II. Soap and water for C. difficile. Standard precautions exclude sweat only.
  • Eye: VA first. Confrontation = fields. Hirschberg = alignment. Swinging flashlight = RAPD. Goldmann = IOP gold standard. Absent red reflex = cataract. Nystagmus = oscillopsia.
  • Ear: healthy ear first, pinna up-back-out, largest speculum. Weber toward the bad ear + negative Rinne = conductive. Epley does NOT test TM movement.
  • Nose breathing → posterior rhinoscopy (mirror up). Mouth breathing and sniffing position → indirect laryngoscopy (mirror down). Wharton's = submandibular.
